chapters.title: Introduction
paragraphs: Three thousand years ago, the world was still young. The continent to the west was a vast wilderness, and most of Europe was home to wild, wandering tribes. Only a few nations, at the eastern end of the Mediterranean and in the nearby parts of Asia, had learned to live in cities, to write, to make their own laws, and to live in a more orderly way. The most brilliant of these nations was Greece. The Greeks were destined to play a great part in the world, in war, learning, government, and the arts, and to become the true founders of our modern civilization. Even while they were still a rough people, they held noble ideals of beauty and courage, of duty and justice. Before they had any writing, their singers were already making songs about their heroes and their great deeds. Fathers taught these songs to their children, and those children taught them to theirs. Later the songs were gathered into two long, wonderful poems, the _Iliad_ and the _Odyssey_, which the world has loved ever since.

The _Iliad_ tells the story of the siege of Ilium, also called Troy, on the western coast of Asia Minor. Paris, a son of the king of Troy, had lured Helen, the most beautiful woman in Greece and the wife of a Greek king, away from her husband’s home. The kings and princes of the Greeks then raised an army and a fleet and sailed across the Ægean Sea to bring her back. For ten years they struggled to take the city. In the grand old legends, the gods themselves joined the war, some taking the side of the Greeks and some the side of the Trojans. In the end it was Ulysses, a famous Greek warrior, brave and fierce but also wise and crafty, who made it possible for the Greeks to capture the city.

The second poem, the _Odyssey_, tells what happened to Ulysses, whom the Greeks called Odysseus, on his way home. He sailed from Troy with his small fleet, whose ships were so small that they moved by oars as well as sails. He was fated to wander for ten more years before he could get back to his rocky island of Ithaca, on the west coast of Greece, and to his faithful wife, Penelope.

His adventures were marvelous, because the gods who had stood against the Greeks at Troy had plotted to bring him bad luck. Just as his ships were safely rounding the southern cape of Greece, a fierce storm blew them off course and carried them to many strange lands. These were lands of giants, man-eating monsters, and wondrous enchantments, which you will enjoy reading about. Through countless dangers the determined wanderer fought his way. He lost ship after ship from his little fleet, and companion after companion from his own crew, until at last he reached home alone and without a friend. There he found his palace, his property, and his family all in the hands of a gang of greedy princes. He defeated them with his cunning and his strength, and his long ordeal was over.

As you read these ancient tales, you must set aside what you know about the world and see it the way the Greeks did. They knew only a small part of it,—the eastern end of the Mediterranean,—yet even that seemed to them a great and marvelous region. Beyond its borders lay strange and mysterious lands full of wonders of every kind, and around it all flowed the great world-river, the encircling stream of Ocean.

The gods lived on Mount Olympus, to the north. There was Zeus, the greatest of them all, god of thunder and the wide heavens; Hera, his wife; Apollo, the god of the bow; Athene, the wise and clever goddess; Poseidon, who ruled the sea; Aphrodite, goddess of love; Hephæstus, the skillful craftsman; Ares, the god of war; Hermes, the swift messenger; and others whom you will come to know as you read. Men worshipped all of them with prayers and sacrifices. As in the early legends of many peoples, the gods often took the form of men and women. They had their favorites and the people they hated, and they decided the fate of mortals however they pleased.

If you let yourselves be drawn into this old, simple way of seeing earth and heaven, you will not only come to love these ancient tales yourself, but you will also see why, century after century, they have been loved longer and better than any other stories, by old and young, by men, women, and children. They are hero-tales,—tales of war and adventure, of courage and nobility, of the heroes whom people have looked up to, almost since the beginning of time, as examples of wisdom, strength, and beauty.
THE ILIAD

chapters.title: The Quarrel
paragraphs: Leda, Queen of Sparta, gave birth to a daughter named Helen, who grew up to be the most beautiful woman on earth. Helen married Menelaus, son of Atreus, and lived in peace with him for a while. They had a daughter, Hermione. But then a man named Paris came to the court of Menelaus, who was by now King of Sparta. Paris was the second son of Priam, King of Troy. Menelaus welcomed him as a guest, but Paris repaid that kindness with a wicked act. He carried off the king’s wife, the lovely Helen, and took many of the king’s treasures along with her.
Le’-da. Men-e-la’-us. Ag-a-mem’-non. Her-mi’-o-ne. A’-treus.

Menelaus and his older brother Agamemnon, who was lord over all the Greeks, then went to all the chiefs and begged them to help avenge this wrong. In this way a great army was gathered, a hundred thousand men, with eleven hundred and eighty-six ships.
For nine years the Greeks besieged the city of Troy. They won their battles in the open field, but they could not break through the walls.

By now they had been away from home for many years, and they were short of the things they needed. So it was their habit to leave part of the army to watch the city while the rest raided the towns of the surrounding country. And that is how the great quarrel that brought so much trouble on the army began.

The Greeks plundered the city of Chryse, where there was a temple of Apollo and a priest who served in it. When they divided the loot, they gave King Agamemnon the priest’s daughter Chryseis, along with other gifts. Soon afterward Chryses, the priest, came to the Greek camp to buy his daughter back. He brought a great deal of gold, and on his golden staff he carried the sacred garland, so that men would show him more respect. He went to all the chiefs, first of all to the sons of Atreus, and said:—
Chry’-se. A-pol’-lo. Chry-se’-is. Chry’-ses.
“Please set my dear daughter free and take the ransom for her. In return, may the gods who live on Olympus let you capture the city of Troy and get safely home.”
All the others spoke kindly to him and were ready to do as he asked. Only Agamemnon refused.

“Get out, old man!” he shouted in a great rage. “Don’t let me catch you hanging around by the ships now, or coming back here again, or it will go badly for you, priest or no priest. As for your daughter, I will take her home to Argos once I have captured Troy.”
The old man hurried away, frightened and troubled. He walked in his grief along the shore of the roaring sea and prayed to his god Apollo.
“Hear me, god of the silver bow! If I have ever built you a temple, and offered you the fat of many bulls and rams, then hear me, and make the Greeks pay for my tears with your arrows!”

Apollo heard him. He was angry that men had insulted his priest, and he came down from the top of Olympus, where he lived. The rattle of his arrows as he went was terrible, and he came like night falling across the sky. Then he shot his deadly arrows, first at the dogs and the mules, and then at the men. Soon black smoke was rolling along the whole shore from the woodpiles where the Greeks burned their dead.
O-lym’-pus.

For nine days the god’s arrows flew through the army. On the tenth day Achilles called the people to an assembly. Hera had told him to, because she loved the Greeks and was sorry to see them dying. When everyone had gathered, he stood up in front of them and spoke to Agamemnon.
A-chil’-les. He’-ra.
“It would surely be better to go home than to die here, all of us, by war or by plague. But come, let us ask some prophet or priest or interpreter of dreams why Apollo is so angry with us.”
Then Calchas stood up. He was the best of the prophets and knew what had been, what was, and what was to come. He spoke.
Cal’-chas. seer, prophet.

“Achilles, you ask me to tell the people why Apollo is angry with them. Listen, I will tell you, but first you must swear to protect me. I know that what I say will anger King Agamemnon, and it goes badly for ordinary men when kings are angry.”
“Speak up, wise man!” said Achilles. “I swear by Apollo that as long as I live, no one will lay a hand on you. Not even Agamemnon himself will, though he is lord of the Greeks.”

The blameless seer took courage and spoke. “Apollo is not angry because of any broken vow or missing offering. He is angry for the sake of his servant the priest, who came to ransom his daughter. Agamemnon treated him with contempt and would not let the girl go. Now you must send her back to her father without any ransom, and with her a hundred animals for sacrifice. Only then will the plague end.”
Agamemnon jumped to his feet in a fury, his eyes blazing like fire.

“You have never once said anything good about me,” he cried, “you prophet of doom! And now you tell me to give up this girl! Very well, I will do it, because I don’t want the people to die. But make sure, Greeks, that I get a share of the loot in her place. It would be wrong for the lord of the whole army to be the only one left without his share.”

“My lord Agamemnon,” cried Achilles, “you are far too greedy for gain. We have no treasure from which to make up your loss. What we took from the towns we have already sold or divided, and it would not be right to make the people hand back what was given to them. Give up the girl now, with no conditions. When we have captured Troy, we will pay you back three and four times over.”

“No, great Achilles,” said Agamemnon, “you won’t cheat me like that. If the Greeks give me a fair share, well and good. If not, I will take one for myself, from you, or from Ajax, or from Ulysses. I will have my share. But we can discuss that later. For now, let us make sure the girl is sent back. Get a ship ready, put her on it, and with her a hundred animals for sacrifice. Let one of the chiefs go with the ship and see that everything is done properly.”
A’-jax.

Then Achilles cried out, his face as dark as a thundercloud: “You are completely shameless and greedy, and truly a bad ruler of men. I have no quarrel with the Trojans. They never stole cattle or sheep of mine in my homeland, because many mountains and a wide stretch of roaring sea lie between us. But I have been fighting for your cause and your brother’s. You don’t care about that at all. You leave me to do the fighting while you sit at ease in your tent. And when the loot is divided, you always get the lion’s share. My own share is small enough, and now, apparently, you mean to take that away too! I have made up my mind to go home. I have no wish to pile up goods and gold for you while I am dishonored myself.”

King Agamemnon answered: “Go, and take your Myrmidons with you! I have other chieftains as good as you, who are ready, as you are not, to show me proper respect, and Zeus is on my side. I hate you, because you always love war and fighting. And as for the loot, know that I will take your share, the girl Briseis, and I will fetch her myself if I have to, so that everyone will know I am the supreme lord here among the Greeks.”
Myr-mi-dons, the soldiers of Achilles. Bri-se’-is.

Achilles was wild with anger. He thought to himself, “Should I get up and kill him, or should I hold back my rage?” As he was thinking, he put his hand on the hilt of his sword and had half pulled it from its sheath, when suddenly the goddess Athene stood behind him. Hera, who loved both chieftains, had sent her. Athene grabbed him by his long yellow hair. Achilles was amazed to feel the powerful grip. He turned, looked, and recognized the goddess, though no one else in the assembly could see her. His eyes flashed terribly as he cried: “Have you come, child of Zeus, to watch Agamemnon’s insolence? I truly believe he will die for his foolishness.”
A-the’-ne.

But Athene said: “No, I have come down from heaven to calm your anger, if you will listen to me. White-armed Hera sent me, because she loves and cares for you both equally. Do not draw your sword, but say as many bitter words as you like. I tell you truly that because of today’s insolence, he will one day bring you splendid gifts, three and four times as much as he takes from you now. Only hold yourself back and do as I say.”

Achilles answered: “I will obey your command, in spite of my anger, because the man who listens to the immortal gods is listened to by them in turn.” As he said this, he rested his heavy hand on the hilt and pushed the sword back into its sheath, and Athene went back to Olympus.

Then he turned to King Agamemnon and spoke again, because his anger was not spent: “You drunkard, with the eyes of a dog and the heart of a deer! You never fight in the front of the battle, and you never dare to join an ambush! I tell you this, and I back my words with a mighty oath: I swear by this scepter. Once it was a branch on a tree. As surely as it will never again have bark or leaves or shoots, so surely will the Greeks one day long for Achilles, when they fall in heaps before the terrible Hector. And you will eat your heart out with rage, thinking how you wronged the bravest man in your army.”

As he spoke, he threw the scepter to the ground and sat down. On the other side, Agamemnon sat there in furious anger. Then Nestor got up. He was an old man of a hundred years and more, and he urged them to make peace. He asked them to listen to his advice. In the old days, he said, great chiefs, men no one alive today would dare to fight, had listened to him. Agamemnon should not take the prize of war away from the bravest of the Greeks, and Achilles, though he was mightier in battle than any other man, should not fight with Agamemnon, who was supreme lord of all the armies of Greece. But he spoke in vain. Agamemnon answered:—

“Nestor, you speak well, and peace is good. But this fellow wants to be master over everyone, and I think there are some who will not obey him. The immortal gods may have made him a great warrior, but does that give him permission to say outrageous things? He must be taught that there is at least one man here who is better than he is.”

Achilles answered: “I would be a slave and a coward if I accepted you as my lord. Give orders to other men, but don’t think you can give them to me. As for the prize the Greeks gave me, let them do what they want with it. They gave it, so let them take it back. But if you dare lay a hand on anything else that belongs to me, then in that hour your blood will stain my spear red.”

With that the assembly broke up. Chryseis was sent home with proper offerings for the god, and the wise Ulysses went with her. All the people washed themselves clean, and made sacrifices to the gods, and the sweet smell of the offerings rose to heaven in curling smoke.
But King Agamemnon would not give up his plan. He called for his heralds, Talthybius and Eurybates, and told them:
Tal-thyb’-i-us. Eu-ryb’-a-tes.

“Heralds, go to the tents of Achilles and bring back the girl Briseis. If he refuses to hand her over, tell him I will come myself, with many men, to take her, and that it will go worse for him then.”

The heralds went, but sorely against their will. They walked along the seashore until they reached the place where the tents of Achilles stood among the Myrmidons. They found him sitting between his tent and his ship. He was not glad to see them, and they stood there frightened and ashamed. But in his heart he knew why they had come, and he called out: “Come closer, heralds, messengers of gods and men. It is no fault of yours that you have come on an errand like this.”

Then he turned to Patroclus, his dearest friend, and said: “Bring the girl out of her tent and let the heralds take her away. But let them bear witness, before gods and men and before this wicked king, that a day will come when he badly needs me to save his army from destruction.”
Pa-tro’-clus.

So Patroclus brought the girl out of her tent and gave her to the heralds, and they led her away, very much against her will. Achilles left his companions and sat down alone on the seashore. He burst into bitter tears, and stretched out his hands and prayed aloud to his mother, Thetis, the daughter of the sea. She heard him, down in the depths where she sat beside her father, the old god of the sea. She rose out of the gray water like a mist, came to where he sat weeping, stroked him with her hand, and spoke his name.
The’-tis.
“What is wrong, my son?” she asked.
He told her the whole story of how he had been wronged, and when he finished he said:

“Please go up to the top of Olympus, to the palace of Zeus. I have often heard you boast of how, long ago, you helped him when the other gods wanted to put him in chains. You brought Briareus of the hundred hands to sit beside him in all his strength, and the gods were afraid to touch Zeus. Go now, remind him of this, and ask him to help the Trojans and give them victory in battle. Then, as the Greeks run before the Trojans, they will enjoy what their king has brought them, the king who has wronged the bravest man in his army.”
Bri-a’-re-us.

His mother answered: “Your lot is a hard one, my son. Your life is short, and it ought to be free of tears and full of joy; instead it seems to me both short and sad. But I will go to Olympus, to the palace of Zeus, as you ask. Not now, though, because he and the other gods have gone to a feast with the pious Ethiopians that lasts twelve days. When he comes back I will beg him and win him over. In the meantime, stay where you are, and don’t go out to battle.”

Meanwhile Ulysses was approaching Chryse with the sacred offerings. When they sailed into the harbor, they folded the sail and stowed it in the ship, lowered the mast, and rowed to the mooring place. They threw out the anchor stones and tied the ropes at the stern. Then they went ashore, carrying the offerings and the girl Chryseis. They brought her to the altar and placed her in her father’s arms, and the wise Ulysses said: “Look. Agamemnon, king of men, sends your daughter back to you, and with her a hundred animals for sacrifice, so that we may win back the favor of the god who has struck the Greeks down in his anger.”

The priest took back his daughter with great joy. When the animals had been set in a ring around the altar, he prayed: “Hear me, God of the silver bow! Once before you listened to my prayer and brought terrible suffering on the Greeks. Hear me now, and put an end to the plague that has fallen on them.”
That was his prayer, and the god listened.

Then they killed the cattle, skinned them, and burned an offering to the gods. They cut up the rest and carefully roasted the pieces on spits. When that was done they ate their meal, and no one went without his share. After the meal, they poured a little wine into the cups as an offering to the gods. Then they stayed until sunset, singing a hymn to the Archer God and enjoying themselves, and he heard their voices and was pleased.

When the sun went down they slept beside the stern ropes. At dawn they went aboard, raised the mast and spread the sail, and Apollo sent them a favorable wind. The dark blue waves hissed around the ship as she sailed, and so they came back to the camp of the Greeks.
All this time Achilles sat angrily beside his ships. He did not go to the war or to the assembly. He sat there, eating his heart out, because he longed to hear the shouts of battle.

chapters.title: The Assembly
paragraphs: On the twelfth day, Thetis rose out of the sea and went up to high Olympus. There she found Zeus sitting by himself on the highest peak. She knelt before him, clasped his knees with her left hand, took hold of his beard with her right, and made her prayer to him.

“Father Zeus, if I have ever helped you by word or deed, grant my prayer now. I beg you, give honor to my son Achilles, whose life is so short. Agamemnon has just brought shame on him by taking away the gift that the Greeks gave him. So grant, I ask you, that the men of Troy win the victory for a while, so that the Greeks will come to honor my son.”

Zeus sat silent for a long time, and Thetis would not let go of him. Then she spoke again: “Give me your promise and confirm it with a nod, or else refuse me. Then I will know that I am the least honored of all the gods.”

Zeus answered, very troubled: “This is a hard thing you ask, because you will set me against Hera, and she will scold me bitterly. Even now she is always complaining that I take the side of the Trojans in battle. So go away now, so that she does not find out you were here, and I will think about how this can best be done. And now, to make you sure of my promise, I will nod. When I nod, the thing cannot be taken back or left undone.”
With that he nodded his dark brows, the hair waved on his head, and all of Olympus shook.

Then Thetis dived down into the deep sea, and Zeus went to his own house, where all the gods rose to greet him. When he sat on his throne, Hera, who knew that Thetis of the silver feet had been talking with him in private, spoke to him angrily.
“Who has been plotting with you? You schemer! Whenever I am away, you love making secret plans, and you never tell me freely what you are thinking.”

The father of gods and men replied: “Hera, don’t imagine that you can know all my thoughts. That would be too hard for you, even though you are my wife. You will be the first to hear whatever is fitting for you to hear. But don’t ask about the plans I make on my own.”

Hera answered: “What are you saying? I have not pried into your plans. You make them just as you please. But now I am very much afraid that Thetis of the silver feet has talked you around. At dawn I saw her kneeling before you. I have no doubt you have promised that Achilles shall be honored, and that many of the Greeks shall die beside their ships.”

Zeus replied: “Nothing escapes you, you witch. But if it is as you say, then that is what I want. Sit down, be quiet, and obey. Otherwise not all the gods on Olympus can save you when I lay on you the hands that no one can resist.”

Hera was frightened, and fell silent, and all the gods were uneasy. But her son Hephæstus, the smith, spoke up: “This will be a sad business indeed, if the two of you quarrel over mortal men and stir up trouble among the gods. If bad feeling like this wins out, how will we enjoy our feasts? Now I will advise my mother to make peace with Zeus, so that he does not scold her again. If he wanted to throw her out of these seats, who could stand against him?”
He-phæs’-tus.

Then he put the double-handled cup into his mother’s hand and said: “Be patient, mother, however upset you are, or I will see you beaten before my eyes, and I could not help you. Once before, when I tried to rescue you, he grabbed me by the foot and flung me from the threshold of heaven. I fell all day long, and at sunset I landed on Lemnos.”

Then Hera smiled and took the cup from her son. He went around to all the other gods, moving from left to right as a cupbearer should, and poured the nectar from the mixing bowl. The blessed gods burst into endless laughter when they saw the limping Hephæstus puffing his way through the hall.

Gods and men slept that night, all but Zeus, who lay thinking how he could do honor to Achilles. At last he decided it was best to send a deceiving dream to Agamemnon. So he said: “Go, deceiving Dream, to the swift ships of the Greeks and find the tent of Agamemnon. Tell him to hurry and arm the Greeks, because he will surely capture the city of Troy.”
So the dream went to Agamemnon’s tent and found him wrapped in sleep. It took the shape of Nestor, the old chief whom the King honored above all others.

The false Nestor said: “Are you sleeping, Agamemnon? Kings should not sleep the whole night through, because they must think of many people and have many cares. Now listen to the words of Zeus: ‘Draw up the army in battle order against Troy. The gods are now of one mind, the day of doom has come for the city, and you will capture it and win everlasting glory.’”

Agamemnon believed the dream. He got out of bed, put on his tunic, threw a great cloak over it, and tied sandals on his feet. He hung his mighty silver-studded sword from his shoulders and took in his right hand the great scepter of his house, the sign of his rule over all the Greeks.

First he called the chiefs together beside the ship of King Nestor, and when they were seated he said: “Listen, my friends. A dream came to me in my sleep tonight, and it looked very much like Nestor. It stood above my head and said: ‘You are sleeping, son of Atreus. Kings should not sleep the whole night through. Now listen to me. I come to you from Zeus, who cares for you though he is far away. He tells you to call the Greeks to battle, because now you will capture the city of Troy.’ That is what the Dream said. So come, let us rouse the Greeks. But first I will test their spirit by urging them to flee home, and you must talk them out of it.”

Then Nestor stood up in his place and said: “If anyone else had told us this dream, we would have thought it false. But since the man who saw it is the chief among us, let us call the people to arms.”

The heralds made the announcement, and the people hurried to their places. They came marching from the ships and the tents to the meeting place, like bees swarming out of a hollow rock and clustering around the spring flowers, some flying this way and some that. The confusion and the uproar were great. Nine heralds tried to quiet the crowd so that they could hear the kings speak, and at last the Greeks stopped shouting and sat down in their places.

Then Agamemnon stood up, holding the scepter in his hand, and spoke: “My friends, Zeus has treated me badly. He promised me that I would capture the city of Troy and then return home. But his words were deceitful, because now he tells me to go back to Argos. Nine years have passed. The timbers of our ships are rotting and the ropes are worn, and our wives and children sit at home waiting for us. So come, let us flee to the land of our fathers, because we cannot take Troy.”

So the King spoke, and he stirred the hearts of the people, or rather, of all who did not know his secret plan. The whole assembly was moved like the sea when the east wind whips up the waves, or like a field of grain when the strong west wind sweeps over it and bends the ears. They ran shouting to the ships and laid hands on them to drag them down to the water.

The Greeks would then have gone home. But Hera said to Athene: “Will the Greeks really run away to their homes like this? And will they leave Helen to Priam and to Troy, Helen, for whom so many have died far from their own country? Hurry, and turn them from this purpose.”

So Athene hurried down from Olympus and found Ulysses. He had not laid a hand on his ship, because grief had struck him to the heart. She said to him: “Son of Laertes, will you really flee to your homeland and leave Helen, for whom so many have died, as a trophy for Priam and the men of Troy? Go now, talk the Greeks out of it, and do not let them drag their ships to the sea.”
La-er’-tes.

When Ulysses heard the goddess’s voice, he threw off his cloak and ran. King Agamemnon gave him his scepter, and carrying it he went among the ships. Whenever he met a chief, he spoke to him gently: “Wait, sir. It does not suit you to be a coward. Sit still and hold the people back. You don’t know the King’s mind. He was only testing the spirit of the Greeks. Don’t anger him, or he may do the people some harm.”
But when he met a common man, he struck him with the scepter and said: “You there, sit still and listen to your betters. There must be one master, one king, the man to whom Zeus has given authority.”
That is how he turned them from their purpose. They hurried back to the assembly, making a noise like a wave breaking on the shore.

When everyone else was quiet, only Thersites kept jeering at the princes, hoping to make the Greeks laugh. He was the ugliest man who had come to Troy: bandy-legged, lame in one foot, with a hump on his back, a narrow chest, and a misshapen head covered in straggly hair. Now he shouted loudly, abusing Agamemnon:
Ther-si’-tes.

“What more do you want, son of Atreus? Your tents are full of bronze, and you have plenty of beautiful women, all given to you by us. Do you want even more? A leader of men should not drag the Greeks into trouble. And the rest of you, who act more like women than men, why don’t you sail home and leave this man to enjoy his plunder by himself? He has just wronged Achilles, taking away his prize—Achilles, a far better man than he is. Achilles must have a mild temper, or this, son of Atreus, would have been your last wrong!”

At that Ulysses rose and stood beside him, and spoke angrily: “Quiet, you babbler. Don’t speak the name of kings, and don’t sneer at your betters. Listen to me: if I hear you talking nonsense again as you have today, I will tear the cloak and tunic off your back and chase you to the ships with shameful blows.” As he said this, he struck the man across the back and shoulders with the scepter, and a bloody welt rose under the blow. Dazed, the fellow cowered down and wiped away his tears.

The others laughed heartily, and one said to his neighbor: “Ulysses has done many good things, but never anything better than this, shutting up this babbler’s mouth. He won’t be insulting the kings again.”
Then Ulysses stood up to speak with the scepter in his hand. Athene stood at his side in the form of a herald, telling the people to be silent so that everyone, near and far, could hear what he said.

“Now, O King,” he said, “the Greeks are bringing shame on you. They are no longer keeping the promise they made when they left Argos, that they would not go home until they had taken the city of Troy. It is true that the hardship here is enough to make us sick at heart and long to go home. A man grows weary if winter winds and stormy seas keep him from his wife for even a single month, and we have been here for nine times twelve months. Still, it is wrong to stay so long and then go back with nothing. You all remember the prophecy given when we sailed from Greece—all of you whom death has not taken away—that we would make war for nine years and in the tenth take the beautiful city of Troy. So stay, Greeks, until you have captured Priam’s mighty town.”
When he finished, all the Greeks shouted their agreement, and the ships echoed the shout back like thunder.

Then King Agamemnon stood up and said: “Go and eat now, and afterward we will join the battle. Let every man sharpen his spear well, fix his shield, feed his horses plenty, and check his chariot, so that we can fight all day long and not stop for a moment until night comes and parts the armies. The strap of the shield will be wet with sweat, the hand that holds the spear will be tired, and the horses that pull the polished chariots will lather. And any man who holds back from the fight and lingers at the ships will find that nothing can save him from becoming food for the dogs and the birds of the air.”

The Greeks shouted once more. They quickly scattered among the ships and tents and ate their meal. Agamemnon held a feast and invited the chiefs: Nestor, Idomeneus, Ajax the Greater, Ajax the Less, Diomed, and Ulysses. Menelaus came without an invitation, knowing he would be welcome.
I-do’-me-neus. Di’-o-med.

Then King Agamemnon stood and prayed: “O Zeus, do not let the sun set and darkness fall until I have brought Priam’s roof down in the dust, burned his doors with fire, and torn the tunic of Hector from his chest!”
That was his prayer, but Zeus did not listen.

When the feast was over, the chiefs lined up their armies for battle. Athene swept through the middle of the host, urging the men on, and she stirred a love of fighting in every heart, so that there was no man who would not have chosen war over going home. The flash of their weapons and armor as they streamed onto the field was like the blaze of a great fire burning a forest on a hilltop. And just as huge flocks of wild geese, cranes, or swans wheel and settle again in the great Asian marsh, or as bees swarm in spring when the milk pails are full, so thickly did the Greeks crowd onto the great plain beside the river Scamander.
Sca-man’-der.

chapters.title: The Duel of Paris and Menelaus
paragraphs: Now the armies came close to battle. The men of Troy advanced with loud cries, noisy as a flock of cranes flying south to escape the winter and the rain. The Greeks marched in silence, determined to stand by one another in the fight, and under their feet a great cloud of dust rose, as thick as the mist the south wind brings over the mountaintops.

They were just about to fight when Paris rushed out from the Trojan ranks. He wore a panther’s skin over his shoulders and carried a bow and a sword, with a spear in each hand, and he called out to the Greeks to send their bravest man to fight him. When Menelaus saw him, he was glad, for he said he would now be avenged on the man who had wronged him so. He jumped from his chariot and ran to meet his enemy. But Paris was afraid when he saw Menelaus, and he fled back among his comrades, like a man who suddenly steps back when he comes upon a snake in a mountain glen. Hector saw this and scolded him: “You are handsome to look at, Paris, but worth nothing. The Greeks will laugh at us if they think you are our bravest warrior just because you look so impressive. But you are a coward. And yet you dared to cross the sea and carry off the beautiful Helen. Why don’t you stand and face the charge of her husband and see what kind of man he is? Your harp, your long hair and your fair face will do you little good when you are lying in the dust! The sons of Troy are a cowardly people, or they would have stoned you long ago.”

Paris answered: “You speak well, Hector, and your rebuke is fair. Your heart is like iron, always set on battle. Yet beauty and love are also gifts of the gods, and they should not be despised. Now, put Menelaus and me in the middle, and let us fight man to man for the beautiful Helen and all her possessions. If he beats me, let him take her and the treasure and leave, and the Greeks with him, and let you live in peace. But if I win, they must leave without her.”

Hector was glad. He walked out in front of the Trojan ranks, holding his spear by the middle, and held his men back. The Greeks would have shot arrows and hurled stones at him, but Agamemnon called out, “Stop! Hector has something to say to us.”

Then Hector said: “Hear me, Trojans and Greeks, and hear what Paris says, Paris who has caused this quarrel between us: ‘Let everyone lay down their weapons, and let Menelaus and me fight for the beautiful Helen and all her wealth. Whichever of us is the better man will keep her and the treasure, and the rest will swear loyalty and friendship.’”

Then Menelaus stood up and spoke: “Listen to me, for this trouble touches me more closely than any of you. The Greeks and the men of Troy want peace, because they have suffered terribly over my quarrel and the wrong Paris did me. So the two of us will fight, and let the one who is fated to die be the one to perish. Men of Troy, bring two sheep, a white ram for the sun and a black ewe for the earth, and we will bring another for Zeus. And let Priam himself come to make the sacrifice and take the oath. Young men are always changeable, but when an old man is among them, he thinks of everyone’s good.”
So Menelaus spoke, and both armies were glad, hoping to see the end of the war.

Hector then sent a herald to the city to summon Priam to the sacrifice and to fetch the sheep. While he was gone, Iris came to Helen in the form of Laodice, the loveliest of Priam’s daughters. Helen was sitting in her hall weaving a large double-width web dyed purple, on which she had worked many battles between the Greeks and the men of Troy. Iris came close and said:
La-o’-di-ce.

“Come, dear sister, and see this marvel. Until now the Greeks and the men of Troy have been fighting on the plain, but now they are sitting in peace and the war has stopped. Paris and Menelaus are going to fight for you, and you will be the wife of the winner.”
So the goddess spoke, and she stirred in Helen a sweet longing for her former husband, her city and her parents. Helen wrapped herself in white clothes and left her room.

Meanwhile Priam was sitting on the wall with the old men. They were too old for war, but they were admirable speakers, like crickets sitting in a tree in the woods and sending out a thin, sweet song. As they talked, the beautiful Helen came near, and they said: “No wonder men suffer so much for such a woman, for she is truly as lovely as a goddess! Still, let her leave in the ships, and not bring a curse on us and our children.”

But Priam called to her: “Come close, my daughter, so you can see the man who was your husband, and your friends and kinsmen. I don’t blame you, because it isn’t you, it is the gods who have brought all this trouble. But tell me, who is that warrior I see, so handsome and strong? There are others a head taller than he, but none with such a noble bearing.”

Helen answered: “Ah, my father! I owe you great respect, yet I wish I had died before I left my husband and child to follow your son. As for this warrior, he is Agamemnon, a good king and a brave soldier, and he was my brother-in-law in the old days.”

“Fortunate Agamemnon,” said Priam, “to rule so many men! I have never seen such an army gathered together. But who is that one, not as tall as Agamemnon but broader in the shoulders? His armor lies on the ground, and he walks through the ranks of his men like a great ram moving through a flock of sheep.”
“That,” said Helen, “is Ulysses of Ithaca, who is wiser and more cunning than any other man.”

“You speak truly, lady,” said Antenor. “I remember Ulysses well, from when he came here on a mission about you with the brave Menelaus. They were my guests, and I came to know them. I remember that in the assembly of the Trojans, when both were standing, Menelaus was taller, but when they sat, Ulysses looked the more majestic. When they got up to speak, Menelaus said only a few words, but said them wisely and well. As for Ulysses—you would have thought him a fool, the way he gripped his scepter stiffly and kept his eyes on the ground. But as soon as he began, oh, what a mighty voice, and what words, falling thick as snow!”
An-te’-nor.
Then Priam asked, “Who is that sturdy hero, so tall and strong, towering over the rest by a head and shoulders?”

“That,” said Helen, “is mighty Ajax, the bulwark of the Greeks. Next to him is Idomeneus. In the old days, when he came from Crete, Menelaus often had him as a guest. I can see all the other chiefs and could name every one. But I can’t see my own dear brothers, Castor, the horse tamer, and Pollux, the mighty boxer. Either they did not come from Sparta, or they came and now avoid the company of men because they are ashamed of me.”
So she spoke, not knowing that they were already sleeping their last sleep, far away in their beloved homeland.

Meanwhile the heralds were bringing the sheep from the town, along with wine in a goatskin, and Idæus the herald carried a bowl and golden cups. He came to King Priam and told him that the armies were calling for him. Priam went, and he and King Agamemnon, one on each side, for the Trojans and the Greeks, made a covenant with a sacrifice: Paris and Menelaus would fight each other, and the beautiful Helen, with all her treasures, would go with whichever of them won.
I-dæ’-us.

When the sacrifice and prayers were over, King Priam said: “I will go back to Troy, because I could not bear to watch my son fight Menelaus. Which of the two is fated to die, only Zeus and the immortal gods know.”
With that he climbed into his chariot, took the reins, and drove back to Troy the way he had come.

Afterward Hector and Ulysses marked out a space for the fight. Hector shook two pebbles in a helmet, looking away as he shook them, so that whoever’s pebble jumped out first would be the first to throw his spear. It turned out that Paris’s lot jumped out first. Then the two warriors put on their armor and came into the space and stood facing each other, brandishing their spears, with hatred in their eyes. Paris threw his spear first. It struck the shield of Menelaus but did not pierce it, because the point bent back. Then Menelaus prayed to Zeus: “Father Zeus, let me take revenge on Paris, who has wronged me, so that men in future ages will fear to wrong their host.” With that, he hurled his long-shafted spear. It hit the shield of Paris and went right through it, then through the breastplate and through the tunic, but Paris leaned aside and the spear did not wound him. Then Menelaus drew his silver-studded sword and struck a mighty blow on the top of Paris’s helmet, but the sword broke into four pieces in his hand. In his anger he cried out, “O Zeus, most spiteful of the gods, I threw my spear in vain, and now my sword is broken.” Then he rushed forward, seized Paris by the helmet, and dragged him toward the Greek army, since the helmet strap was choking Paris. And he would truly have captured him, but Aphrodite undid the strap under the chin, and the helmet came off in Menelaus’s hand. Menelaus swung it around among the Greeks and charged again with another spear in his hand. But Aphrodite snatched Paris away, hid him in a mist, and set him down in his room in Troy. Menelaus searched for him everywhere, but no one could tell him where he was. No son of Troy would have hidden him out of kindness, for they all hated him like death.
Aph-ro-di’-te.
Then King Agamemnon said, “So, men of Troy, the next step is yours. Hand back the beautiful Helen with her treasure, and add a fair payment to me for everything this has cost me in money and effort.”
So King Agamemnon spoke, and the Greeks cheered.

chapters.title: The Broken Oath
paragraphs: Meanwhile the gods were sitting in council in the hall of Zeus. Beautiful Hebe poured out nectar for them, and they toasted one another with golden cups as they looked down on the city of Troy. Then Zeus spoke, trying to provoke Hera with taunting words:—
He’-be.

“Menelaus has two helpers among the goddesses, Hera and Athene. Yet there they sit off to the side, enjoying themselves, while Aphrodite stays close to Paris and saves him from certain death. But Menelaus has won this duel, so let us decide what happens next. Shall we stir up the war again, or make peace between the two armies? If you choose peace, Menelaus can take Helen back to his home, and Priam’s city can go on standing.”

That was what he said. But Hera and Athene sat side by side, seething, and each of them was thinking of ways to hurt the Trojans. Athene stayed silent, though she was furious inside. Hera could not hold in her anger, and she burst out:—

“What kind of talk is this? Do you want to throw away all my work and trouble, everything I went through to gather this army so that Priam and his sons could be destroyed? Do what you like. But the other gods will not be pleased.”

Zeus answered her angrily: “Tell us what Priam and his sons have done to you, that you want so ruthlessly to see this beautiful city of Troy fall. If you could walk in through its gates and eat Priam raw, with all his sons, then perhaps your hatred would finally be satisfied. Very well, do as you like. I won’t let this quarrel come between you and me. But remember what I tell you. If some day I decide to destroy a city that you love, do not say no to me or get in my way, because here I am giving in to you. Of all the cities of men that lie under the stars, I have loved Troy the most. My altar there has never lacked its feasts and offerings, or the sweet smoke that the gods are owed.”

Then Hera replied: “There are three cities that I love: Argos, Sparta, and Mycenæ. If they have offended you, destroy them. I won’t stand in your way, and I could not stop you anyway. But my work should not be wasted either. I, too, am a daughter of Chronos, and I rank first among the immortals, because I am your wife, and you are the King. So come, let us give way to each other, and the other gods will follow us. Send Athene down now, and let her make sure that the Trojans are the ones who start the fighting and break the truce.”
My-ce’-næ.
When she finished, Zeus did not refuse. He turned at once to Athene and said: “Hurry down to the armies, and make sure the Trojans are the ones who break the truce.”

So Athene rushed down from the peak of Olympus. She looked like a star that Zeus sends as a sign to sailors at sea, or to an army marching out to battle, and everyone who sees it is filled with wonder.

She went into the Trojan army, taking the shape of Laodocus, son of Antenor, and found Pandarus standing among his men. Then the false Laodocus said: “Pandarus, will you dare to shoot an arrow at Menelaus? The Trojans would love you for it, and Paris most of all, if they could see Menelaus killed by an arrow from your bow. Take aim, then, but first pray to Apollo, and promise that you will sacrifice a hundred animals when you return to your city.”
La-o’-do-cus. Pan’-da-rus.

Now, Pandarus had a bow made from the horns of a wild goat that he had killed himself. The horns were sixteen palms long, and a skilled craftsman had polished them smooth and fitted a golden tip to hold the bowstring. Pandarus strung the bow while his companions held up their shields to hide him. Then he took an arrow from his quiver, set it on the string, and pulled the string back to his chest until the arrowhead touched the bow, and he let it fly. It was a well-aimed shot, but the gods did not want Menelaus to die. The daughter of Zeus stood in front of him and turned the arrow aside, brushing it away the way a mother brushes a fly off her child while he sleeps. She guided it to the spot where the golden clasps of the belt met and the breastplate overlapped. It went through the belt, through the armor, and through the undergarment, and it broke the skin. Then red blood gushed out and stained his white skin.

King Agamemnon was horrified to see the blood, and so was brave Menelaus, until he saw the barb of the arrow and realized the wound was not deep. But Agamemnon cried out: “It was a bad hour for you, my brother, when I made a treaty with these treacherous Trojans. I know very well that oaths and sacrifices are never in vain. Even if Zeus does not carry out his purpose now, he will take his revenge in the end, and the guilty will pay, they and their wives and their children. Troy will fall. But woe to me if you should die, Menelaus! The Greeks will go straight back to their homeland, and the beautiful Helen will be left behind for the Trojans to boast about. I will be put to shame when one of them jumps on your tomb, Menelaus, and says, ‘The great Agamemnon has gotten his revenge well! He brought an army here, and now he has gone home and left Menelaus behind.’ May the earth swallow me up before that day!”
“No,” said Menelaus. “Don’t be afraid. The arrow only grazed my skin.”
Then King Agamemnon ordered Machaon the physician to be brought. Machaon came, pulled out the arrow, wiped away the blood, and spread healing medicine on the wound.
Ma-cha’-on.

While this was going on, King Agamemnon went all through the army. Whenever he saw someone hurrying to get ready for battle, he praised him and encouraged him. But whenever he saw someone hanging back, dragging his feet, or being lazy, he scolded him sharply, whether he was a common soldier or a chief.

So he went through the whole army. And the Greeks moved forward to the battle like waves that curl up, then crash on the shore and throw foam high into the air. They marched in order behind their chiefs, and they were so quiet that you would have thought they were mute. The Trojans, though, were like a flock of ewes waiting to be milked, bleating when they hear their lambs call. Their army made just such a confused noise, because men of many languages had gathered there. And on both sides the gods urged the soldiers on.

chapters.title: The Valiant Deeds of Diomed
paragraphs: When the armies came together at one spot, they crashed into each other with shields and spears, and there was a huge clash as the shields met. Next came the loud groaning of the men who were struck down and the shouts of the men who beat them, and the ground ran with blood. Think of two rivers swollen with winter rain, pouring their waters together in a deep gorge where the valleys meet, while shepherds far away in the hills hear the roar. That is how the two armies came together, with a mighty noise and great confusion.

Then the Greeks drove the Trojans back, and each of the chiefs killed an enemy. But no one was like Diomed. He raged through the battle so wildly that you could not tell which army he belonged to, the Greeks or the Trojans. Then Pandarus aimed an arrow at him and hit him in the right shoulder as he charged forward. Pandarus shouted: “Forward, brave Trojans! The best of the Greeks is wounded! I think his strength will soon give out, unless Apollo has tricked me.”

He said this in triumph, but the arrow did not stop Diomed. He only jumped down from his chariot and said to his charioteer Sthenelus, “Come down and pull this arrow out of my shoulder.” Sthenelus pulled it out, and blood spurted from the wound. Then Diomed prayed to Athene: “Goddess, if you ever loved my father and stood beside him in the heat of battle, be my friend too. Let me get within a spear’s throw of the man who wounded me and who is bragging over me, saying that I will not be looking at the shining sun much longer.”
Sthen’-e-lus.

So he prayed, and Athene heard him. She made his hands and feet light, stood beside him, and said: “Be bold now, Diomed, and fight the Trojans! I have put into your heart the same spirit that your father had, and I have lifted the mist from your eyes so that you can tell a god from a man. Do not fight any of the immortals if a god should come your way. Only if Aphrodite enters the battle may you wound her.”

Athene said this and went on her way, and Diomed turned back to the battle and joined the front ranks. He had been eager to fight before, but now he was three times as eager. He was like a lion that a shepherd has wounded slightly as it leaps into the sheepfold, but has not killed. The man escapes into his house, and the sheep flee in terror and pile up in a heap. That is how Diomed raged among the Trojans.

Æneas saw him and wondered how he could stop him. He pushed through the army until he found Pandarus. “Pandarus,” he said, “where are your bow and arrows? Look how this man spreads death through our ranks. Shoot at him, but pray to Zeus first.”
Æ-ne’-as.

Then Pandarus answered: “I think that man is Diomed. The shield, the helmet, and the horses are his. But I wonder whether he might be a god. At the very least, some god stands by him and protects him. I just shot an arrow at him and hit him in the shoulder, right through his armor, and I thought I had killed him. But look, I haven’t hurt him at all! And now I don’t know what to do, because I have no chariot here. I came trusting in my bow, and it has failed me twice now. I have hit two of the chiefs, Menelaus and Diomed, and I saw red blood flow from each, yet I haven’t harmed either one. If I ever get home safe, I will break this useless bow.”

“No,” said Æneas, “don’t talk like that. Climb into my chariot and see what kind of horses we have in Troy. They will carry us safely back to the city even if Diomed beats us. You take the reins and the whip, and I will fight. Or, if you like, you fight, and I will drive.”
“No,” said Pandarus. “Let the horses have the driver they know. If we had to turn and flee, they might hold back or bolt, missing their master’s voice, and that could cost us both our lives.”

So Pandarus climbed into the chariot, and the two of them drove together against Diomed. Sthenelus saw them coming and said to his comrades: “I see two mighty warriors. We should go back to our chariot.”

But Diomed frowned and said: “Don’t talk about going back. It is useless to talk to me that way. As for my chariot, I don’t care about it. I will go against these men just as I am. They will not both get back safely, even if one of them escapes. But you keep my chariot right where it is, and tie the reins to the rail. And if I kill these men, climb into the chariot of Æneas and drive it into the Greek army. There are no horses under the sun like these, for they come from the breed that Zeus himself gave to King Tros.”
Meanwhile Pandarus and Æneas were coming closer, and Pandarus threw his spear. It went right through Diomed’s shield and reached his armor, and Pandarus shouted:—
“You are hit in the side. I think this will bring you down.”
“No,” said Diomed. “You missed. You didn’t hit me at all.”

As he said it, he threw his own spear. It went in through Pandarus’s nose, teeth, and tongue and came out under his chin. He fell headfirst from the chariot, and his armor clanged around him. Æneas immediately leaped down with spear and shield to guard his friend’s body, standing over it the way a lion stands over its kill. But Diomed picked up a huge stone, one that two men of our day could hardly carry, and hurled it. It hit Æneas on the hip and crushed the bone. The hero dropped to one knee, clawing at the ground with his hand, and darkness covered his eyes. He would have died that very hour, but his mother Aphrodite caught him in her white arms and wrapped her veil around him. Even so, Diomed did not want to let his enemy get away, and he rushed at her and wounded her on the wrist. Out gushed her blood, the kind of blood that flows in the veins of the immortal gods, who do not eat the food or drink the drink of men. With a loud shriek she dropped her son, but Apollo caught him up and wrapped him in a dark mist, so that none of the Greeks could see him and kill him.
But Diomed shouted after Aphrodite: “Get out of the battle, daughter of Zeus! It is enough for you to trick weak women.”

The goddess ran wildly from the battle. Iris, swift as the winds, took her by the hand and led her out of the crowd, since she was in agony from the pain. She found Ares on the left side of the field and knelt in front of him, begging for his horses with many pleas. “Help me, dear brother,” she said. “Lend me your horses to carry me to Olympus. I am in agony from a wound that a mortal man gave me, Diomed, who would fight even Father Zeus himself.”
A’-res.

Then Ares gave her his chariot, and Iris took the reins and flicked the horses with the whip. They reached Olympus quickly. Iris pulled the horses to a stop, and Aphrodite fell into the lap of her mother Dione, who took her daughter in her arms and stroked her, saying:—
“Dear child, which of the immortals has hurt you like this?”
Aphrodite answered, “No immortal did it, but a mortal man, Diomed, who is now fighting against the immortal gods.”
But Dione answered: “Be brave and bear your pain, for many who live on Olympus have suffered at the hands of mortal men.”
Di-o’-ne.

With that, she wiped the blood from the wound with both hands, and the painful injury was healed. But Hera and Athene looked on and mocked. Athene said to Zeus, “Your daughter must have been persuading one of the Greek women to follow the Trojans, whom she loves so much, and look, she has scratched her hand on the pin of a golden brooch.”
The father only smiled. He called Aphrodite over and said, “My child, war is not your business. Yours are love and marriage. Leave the fighting to Athene and Ares.”

Meanwhile Diomed sprang at Æneas, even though he knew that Apollo himself was protecting him. He paid no attention to the god, because he was eager to kill the hero and strip off his armor. Three times he sprang, and three times Apollo knocked back his shining shield. The fourth time, Apollo warned him in terrible words, “Take care, Diomed, and fall back. Do not think you can match yourself against the gods.” Then Apollo carried Æneas out of the battle and laid him down in his own temple in the citadel of Troy, where his wound was healed. All the while, the Trojans and the Greeks kept fighting over what they thought was his body, because Apollo had made a likeness of the hero and thrown it down among them. Then Sarpedon spoke bitter words to Hector:—
Sar-pe’-don.

“Where is your boasting now, Hector? You said you could defend your city alone, without your people or your allies, with only your brothers and your brothers-in-law. But I don’t see a single one of them. They have slunk off and hidden, like dogs running from a lion. We, your allies, are the ones keeping up the fight. I came a long way to help your people, and I don’t shrink from the battle, but you must do your share.”

These words cut Hector to the heart. He jumped down from his chariot and ran through the army, urging the men to fight. On the other side, the Greeks took fresh courage. Ares brought Æneas back whole from his wound and gave him new strength and spirit. His comrades were very glad to see him, and they asked him no questions, for there was hardly time for questions that day. Many brave deeds were done then, and no one fought more bravely than Æneas.

All this while Hector, with Ares beside him, was spreading death and ruin through the Greek ranks. Hera and Athene saw him from where they sat on the top of Olympus, and they were angry. They went to Father Zeus and asked his leave to stop Hector in his rage. Zeus said, “Do as you like.” So they harnessed the horses to Hera’s chariot and came down to earth. With every stride the horses flew as far as a man can see who sits on a cliff and looks over the sea to where it meets the sky. The goddesses landed at the place where the two rivers join. There they unhitched the horses, and then they flew like doves to where the bravest Greeks stood around King Diomed. Hera took the shape of Stentor, who had lungs of bronze and a voice as loud as fifty men together, and she cried out: “Shame on you, men of Greece! When Achilles was fighting, the Trojans never dared come past their gates. Now they fight far from their city, right up by the ships.” Athene, meanwhile, went to Diomed, who was standing there wiping away the blood from the wound Pandarus had given him with an arrow. She said to him: “The son of Tydeus is not much like his father. Tydeus was small, but he was a fierce fighter. You, though—I can’t tell whether it is tiredness or fear that holds you back—hardly seem to be a true son of Tydeus.”
Ty’-deus.

But Diomed answered: “No, great goddess. I know who you are, daughter of Zeus, and it is not tiredness or fear that holds me back. I am obeying your own command. You told me not to fight any of the immortal gods, except Aphrodite if she came into the battle. So I am giving way, because I see Ares lording it over the ranks of war.”
Then Athene said: “Never mind Ares. Drive your chariot straight at him and strike him with your spear. This very morning he promised to help the Greeks, and now he has changed his mind.”

As she said this, she shoved Sthenelus, who was driving the chariot, so that he jumped out onto the ground. Then she climbed in herself, took the reins, and lashed the horses on. Athene had put on the helmet of Hades, which makes whoever wears it invisible, because she did not want Ares to see who she was. The god saw Diomed coming and hurled his spear over the yoke of the chariot, eager to kill the hero. But Athene caught the spear in her hand and turned it aside, so that it flew harmlessly through the air. Then Diomed thrust with his own spear, and Athene leaned her weight on it, so that it pierced Ares in the belly, just where his belt was fastened. Ares roared with pain, as loud as nine or ten thousand men shouting as they rush into battle. The Greeks and Trojans shook with fear when they heard it. And Diomed saw the god rise up to Olympus like a thundercloud rising when the hot south wind blows.
Ha’-des, the god of the underworld.

Ares sat down beside Zeus and showed him the immortal blood flowing from his wound. He cried: “Father Zeus, can you stand by and watch such deeds? Look at this daughter of yours, how bent she is on evil and mischief. All of us who live on Olympus obey you, but her you never stop, by word or by deed. Now she has egged on this reckless Diomed to vent his madness on the immortal gods. First he wounded Aphrodite on the wrist, and then he came at me. My swift feet carried me away, or I would surely have suffered the pains of death among the corpses of the slain.”

But Zeus frowned at him and said: “Don’t come to me with your complaints. Of all the gods of Olympus, you annoy me the most, because you always love battle and strife. It is your mother Hera who has brought this pain on you. Still, I can’t let you suffer any longer, because you are my child.”
Then Zeus called Pæon the healer and told him to treat the wound, and Pæon took away its pain. Hebe bathed Ares and dressed him in fine clothes, and he sat down beside Zeus, happy again.
Pæ’-on. He’-be.

chapters.title: Glaucus and Diomed
paragraphs: After Ares had gone, the Greeks gained the upper hand again and killed many of the Trojans and their allies. At last Helenus, the wise seer, spoke to Hector and Æneas:—
Glau’-cus. Hel’-e-nus.

“Make the army fall back to the walls. Go through the ranks and give the men as much strength and courage as you can. And you, Hector, when you have done that, go into the city. Tell your mother to gather the women of Troy and take the most costly robe she owns, and lay it on the knees of Athene in her temple. She should vow to sacrifice twelve heifers, in case Athene will take pity on us and keep this Diomed away from our walls. No Greek is as strong as he is. We didn’t fear even Achilles himself as much as we fear this man today, he is so terrible and fierce. Go now, and we will hold our ground here as well as we can.”
Then Hector went through the ranks, telling the men to take heart, and set off for the city.

When he had gone, Glaucus and Diomed met in the open ground between the two armies. Diomed spoke first: “Tell me, brave man, which of mortal men are you? I have never seen you in battle before. Yet now you have come out far in front of your comrades, and you are willing to face my spear. If you are one of the immortal gods and have come down from heaven, I will not fight you. I wouldn’t dare to take on the gods of heaven.”

Glaucus answered him: “Brave son of Tydeus, why do you ask my name and my family, and the generations of my ancestors? The generations of men are like the leaves of the forest. The wind scatters them on the ground, and the forest grows new ones in the spring. So it is with the generations of men: one passes away, and another comes. But if you want to know these things, listen. I am the son of Hippolochus, who was the son of Bellerophon.”
Hip-pol’-o-chus. Bel-ler’-o-phon.

When Glaucus had spoken, Diomed was glad at heart. He stuck his spear into the ground and spoke kindly to the prince: “Then you are a friend of my family by inheritance. Long ago, great Œneus had Bellerophon as a guest in his house for twenty days. They gave each other fine gifts. Œneus gave Bellerophon a belt richly embroidered with purple, and Bellerophon gave Œneus a golden cup with a mouth on each side. I left that cup behind in my palace at home when I came here. Now, Œneus was my grandfather. So I am your friend and host when you come to the land of Argos, and you are mine if I ever come to Lycia. But for now, let us each avoid the other’s spear, even in the thickest of the fighting. There are many Trojans and many of their brave allies whom I can kill, if the gods put them in my hands and my feet are quick enough to catch them. And you have many Greeks to kill, if you can. But now let us trade armor, so that both the Greeks and the Trojans will know that we are friends by inheritance.”
Œ’-neus. Lyc’-i-a.

So Tydeus’s son spoke. The two chiefs jumped down from their chariots, clasped each other’s hands, and pledged their word. Then Zeus took away Glaucus’s good sense and made him foolish, so that he gave his armor for Diomed’s: gold for bronze, the worth of a hundred oxen for the worth of nine.

chapters.title: Hector and Andromache
paragraphs: Hector came into the city by the Scæan gates. As he went, wives and mothers crowded around him, asking how their husbands and sons had fared. He said nothing, except to tell them to pray. There was indeed terrible news for many of them, if he had told what he knew. Then he came to the palace of King Priam, and there he saw his mother Hecuba, and with her Laodice, the loveliest of her daughters. Hecuba took him by the hand and said:—
An-drom’-a-che. Scæ’-an. Hec’-u-ba.

“Why have you left the battle, my son? Are the Greeks pressing you hard, and do you want to pray to Father Zeus from the citadel? Let me bring you honey-sweet wine to pour out for him, and to drink yourself, to cheer your heart.”

But Hector said: “Don’t give me wine, mother. It would weaken my knees and make me forget my courage. And I must not pour an offering to Zeus like this, with unwashed hands. Instead, gather the mothers of Troy and go to the temple of Athene. Take the most precious and beautiful robe in your storerooms and lay it on the goddess’s knees, and ask her to keep this terrible Diomed away from the walls of Troy. Don’t forget to vow twelve heifers as a sacrifice as well. As for me, I will go and find Paris, to see if he will come with me to the war. I wish the earth would open and swallow him up, for he is truly a curse to King Priam and to Troy.”

Queen Hecuba went into her house and ordered her maids to gather the old women of the city. Then she went to her storeroom, where the finely woven robes were kept, the work of Sidonian women, which Paris himself had brought from Sidon when he sailed across the wide sea, bringing noble Helen home with him. The queen picked the loveliest robe of all. It shone like a star, and it lay at the very bottom of the pile.
Si-do’-ni-an. Si’-don.

When she and the old women with her reached the temple of Athene on the citadel, the priestess of Athene opened the doors for them. They raised their hands and cried out, and the priestess laid the robe on the goddess’s knees and prayed:—

“Lady Athene, protector of the city, break Diomed’s spear now, and let him fall on his face before the Scæan gates. If you will take pity on our town, and on the wives and little children of the Trojans, then we will sacrifice twelve heifers to you that have never felt the goad.”
So she prayed, but Athene paid no attention to her words.

Meanwhile Hector went to Paris’s house, which stood on the citadel near his own home and Priam’s. He found Paris busy with his weapons, and the beautiful Helen sat near him, giving out tasks to her maids.

When Hector saw his brother, he spoke bitterly to him and taunted him, as though Paris were staying out of the battle because he was angry. “You are wrong to be angry. The people are dying around the walls, and the war is blazing around the city, all because of you. Get up, or the city will be burned to the ground.”

Paris answered: “Brother, you are right. I wasn’t sitting here out of anger. I was upset about my bitter defeat. But now my wife has urged me to go into the battle, and she is right, because victory goes first to one side and then to the other. Wait for me while I put on my armor, or if you want to go ahead, I will catch up with you.”

Then Helen spoke to him gently: “My brother, come in and sit down in this chair, because my heart is weary with my guilt and my husband’s guilt. Zeus has given us an evil fate, so that our story will be sung in days still to come.”

But Hector said: “Don’t ask me to rest. I am eager to help the Trojans, for they badly need it. But urge your husband to catch up with me while I am still inside the city, because I am going home now to see my wife and my little son. I don’t know whether I will come back to them again.”

So Hector left and went to his own house to look for his wife Andromache, but he did not find her. She was on a tower of the wall with her child and the child’s nurse, weeping bitterly with fear. Hector said to the maids:—
“Tell me, where has the white-armed Andromache gone? Is she visiting one of my sisters-in-law, or is she at the temple of Athene with the mothers of Troy?”

An old woman, the housekeeper, answered: “She isn’t here. She has gone up to one of the towers on the wall, because word came that the Greeks were beating our men back. She ran off like a madwoman, and the nurse followed with the child in her arms.”

So Hector ran through the city to the Scæan gates, and there Andromache saw him and hurried to meet him. With her was the nurse, carrying the little child against her chest. He was Hector’s only child, and beautiful, with a head as bright as a star. His father called him Scamandrius, after the river, but the Trojans called him Astyanax, the “City-King,” because his father was the one who saved the city. Hector smiled silently when he saw the child, but Andromache clasped his hand and wept, and said:—
Sca-man’-dri-us. As-ty’-a-nax.

“Oh, Hector, your courage will be the death of you. You have no pity for your wife and child, and you don’t spare yourself, and all the Greeks will rush at you and kill you. It would be better for me to die if I lose you, because I have no comfort but you. My father is dead, because Achilles killed him. I had seven brothers, and they all fell in a single day at the hands of the great Achilles. And my mother is dead too. After she had been ransomed, Artemis struck her down with an arrow in her father’s house. But you are my father and my mother and my brother, and my husband as well. Have pity, then, and stay here on the wall, so that you don’t leave me a widow and your child an orphan. And station the army here by this fig tree, where the city is easiest to capture, because the bravest Greeks come against it.”
Ar’-te-mis.

But Hector said, “No, leave these matters to me. I could not bear for any man or woman of Troy to see me hiding from the war. My own heart despises the thought, and it tells me to fight in the front line. I know very well that Priam, and Priam’s people, and holy Troy will fall. Yet it is not the fate of Troy that troubles me most, or of the people, or even of my father and mother. It is you I fear for, on the day some Greek drags you away as a captive, and you must work at the loom or carry water in the land of Greece. Someone will see you then and say, ‘That was Hector’s wife, the wife of the bravest man in Troy.’ May the earth cover me before that day comes!”

Then Hector reached out his arms for his little son. But the child shrank back into his nurse’s arms and cried out loudly, frightened by the gleaming bronze and by the horse-hair plume that nodded so fearsomely on top of the helmet. His father and mother both laughed out loud. Hector took the helmet off his head and set it on the ground. Then he picked up his boy, kissed him, and bounced him in his arms, praying aloud to Father Zeus and all the gods.

“Grant, Father Zeus and all you gods, that this child will grow up to be as I am, great among the people of Troy. May they say of him one day, as he carries home the bloody spoils of war, ‘He is a better man than his father.’ And may his mother be glad at heart.”
Then he handed the child to his mother, and she held him close against her breast and smiled through her tears. Her husband’s heart was moved. He stroked her with his hand and said:

“Do not be too troubled. No man will kill me before my fate says so. And as for fate, I think no man can escape it, whether he is a coward or a brave man. Now go and tend to your work, the shuttle and the loom, and tell your maids to do theirs. Let the men worry about the battle.”

Then Hector picked his helmet up from the ground, and Andromache started for home, looking back again and again. When she got there, she and all her maids wept for Hector as if he were already dead, because she believed she would never see him come safely home from battle again.

As Hector went on his way, Paris came running up, dressed in shining armor. He was like a proud horse that has been well fed in his stall and now gallops across the plain with his head held high and his mane streaming over his shoulders. He said to Hector:
“I’m afraid I have held you up when you were in a hurry, and I did not come when you called.”

Hector answered, “No one can find fault with your courage. But you hold yourself back from the fighting on purpose, and that is why the Trojans speak shamefully of you. Come now, let us go to the war.”
So they went out through the gates together and attacked the Greek armies, killing many famous chiefs. Glaucus the Lycian went with them.

chapters.title: The Duel of Hector and Ajax
paragraphs: Now when Athene saw the Greeks dying at the hands of Hector and his companions, she was deeply grieved. She came down from the heights of Olympus to help them. Apollo met her and said:
“Have you come, Athene, to help the Greeks, whom you love so well? Then let us put an end to the fighting for today. Later they can fight on until the doom of Troy is fulfilled.”
But Athene replied, “How can we stop it?”
Apollo said, “We will urge Hector to challenge the bravest of the Greeks to fight him alone, man against man.”
So the two of them put the idea into the mind of Helenus the seer. Helenus went up to Hector and said:

“Listen to me, for I am your brother. Make the rest of the Trojans and the Greeks sit down, and challenge the bravest of the Greeks to fight you, man against man. You may be sure you will not die in this battle, for the immortal gods have willed it so.”
Hector was overjoyed. He went out in front of the army, holding his spear by the middle, and held the Trojans back. King Agamemnon did the same with his own men. Then Hector spoke:

“Hear me, men of Troy and men of Greece. The agreement we made with each other has been broken, because Zeus wanted it so, planning trouble for both sides, until either you capture our high-walled city or we defeat you at your ships. But now let one of you who call yourselves the Greek champions come forward and fight me, man against man. Let it be agreed that if he beats me, he may strip me of my armor but must give my body back to my people, so they can burn it on a fire. If I beat him, I will strip him of his armor but give his body to the Greeks, so they can bury him and raise a great mound over him beside the broad salt water of the Hellespont. Then people of later days, sailing by, will see it and say, ‘That is the tomb of the bravest of the Greeks, who was killed by Hector.’ That way my name will live forever.”
Hel’-les-pont.
But all the Greeks stayed silent. They were afraid to face him in battle, yet ashamed to hold back. At last Menelaus jumped forward and said:
“You are women, not men! Is there no one who will stand up to this Hector? Look, I will fight him myself.”
He said this in his anger, courting death, because Hector was much stronger than he was. Then King Agamemnon answered:

“No, this is madness, my brother. Do not let your anger push you into fighting a man who is stronger than you. Even Achilles hates to face Hector. Sit down among your comrades, and the Greeks will find some other champion to fight him.”

Menelaus listened to his brother’s words and sat down. Then nine famous chiefs stood up. First was King Agamemnon, lord of many nations. Next came Diomed, son of Tydeus, then Ajax the Greater and Ajax the Less, then Idomeneus and his companion in arms Meriones, then Eurypylus, Thoas, son of Andræmon, and the wise Ulysses.
Me-ri’-o-nes. Eu-ryp’-y-lus. Tho’-as. An-dræ’-mon.
Then Nestor said, “Let us draw lots to decide who will fight the mighty Hector.”

So each chief threw a lot into King Agamemnon’s helmet. The people prayed, “Grant, you gods, that the lot of Ajax the Greater will jump out, or the lot of Diomed, or the lot of King Agamemnon.” Then Nestor shook the helmet, and the lot they wanted most leapt out. The herald carried it along the ranks and showed it to the chiefs, but none of them recognized it as his own until he came to where Ajax the Greater stood among his comrades. Ajax had put his own mark on it, so he reached out his hand, claimed it, and was very glad. He threw it on the ground at his feet and said:
“The lot is mine, my friends, and I am delighted, for I think I will defeat the mighty Hector.”

Then he put on his armor and stepped forward with a grim smile. He came on with great strides, swinging his long spear. All the Greeks were glad to see him, but the Trojans’ knees went weak with fear, and even great Hector’s heart beat fast. He did not tremble or give way, though, since he himself had called for this fight. Ajax came close, holding up his huge shield like a wall. It was made of seven layers of bull’s hide with an eighth layer of bronze. He spoke threateningly:

“Now you will learn, Hector, what kind of men we still have among our chiefs, even though lion-hearted Achilles is far away, sitting idle in his tent, furious with King Agamemnon. So you begin the fight.”

“Do not talk to me,” said Hector, “as if I were a woman or a child who knew nothing about war. I know every trick of battle very well: how to swing my shield this way and that, how to drive my chariot through a tangle of horses, and how to stand and fight hand to hand.”

As he said this, he hurled his long spear and struck the great shield. It went through six layers but was stopped at the seventh. Then Ajax threw his spear and hit Hector’s shield. It went through the shield and the breastplate, and it cut his tunic close against his side, but Hector swerved away and escaped death. Then, each with a fresh spear, they rushed at each other like lions or wild boars of the forest. Hector struck first, hitting the middle of Ajax’s shield, but he did not pierce it, because the spear point bent back. Then Ajax, with a great leap, drove his spear at Hector’s shield and went through it, forcing Hector back and grazing his neck so that dark blood welled out. Still Hector did not give up the fight. He snatched up a big, rough stone from the ground and hurled it at the seven-layered shield. The bronze rang loudly, but the shield did not break. Then Ajax picked up a much heavier stone and threw it with all his strength. It smashed Hector’s shield and knocked him backward, and he fell flat on his back with his shield on top of him. But Apollo lifted him to his feet. Both men then drew their swords, but before they could close in battle, the heralds arrived and held their staffs between them. Idæus, the herald of Troy, said:
I-dæ’-us.
“Stop fighting, my sons. Zeus loves you both, and you are both mighty warriors. We all know that well. But now night is telling you to stop, and it is good to obey it.”
Then Ajax said, “It is for Hector to speak, since he was the one who called the bravest of the Greeks to battle. Whatever he wants, I will do.”
