Hector said, “Ajax, the gods have given you height, strength and skill, and there is no better warrior among the Greeks. Let us stop fighting now. We may meet again, and the gods may give the victory to you or to me. But for now let us exchange gifts, so that Trojans and Greeks will say, ‘Hector and Ajax met in fierce combat and parted as friends.’”

So Hector gave Ajax a silver-studded sword with its scabbard and sword belt, and Ajax gave Hector a small shield splendid with purple. Then they parted. The Trojans were overjoyed to see Hector return safely. The Greeks were glad too, as they led Ajax, delighted with his victory, to King Agamemnon. The king invited the chiefs to a feast and ordered an ox of five years old to be killed. He honored Ajax above all the others, giving him the best cuts of meat. When the feast was over, Nestor said:

“It would be good to stop the war for a while and burn our dead, since so many have fallen. We should also build a great wall with a trench around it, and put in gates wide enough for a chariot to pass through, so that our ships will be safe if the Trojans press us hard.”
But the next morning a herald came from Troy to the chiefs as they sat in council beside King Agamemnon’s ship, and he said:

“This is the message from Priam and the men of Troy. Paris will give back all the treasures he took with fair Helen, and many more besides, but he will not give up fair Helen herself. If that does not satisfy you, grant us a truce so that we can bury our dead.”
Then Diomed spoke. “No, we will not take the treasures. Even a fool can see that the doom of Troy has come.”
King Agamemnon said, “Herald, you have heard the answer of the Greeks. As for the truce, let it be as you wish.”

The next day they burned their dead, and the Greeks built a wall with gates and dug a trench around it. It was finished at sunset, and they were preparing a meal when ships arrived from Lemnos carrying wine. The Greeks bought it, some paying with bronze, some with iron, and some with ox-hide shields. They feasted merrily all night. The Trojans feasted in their city as well. But terrible thunder rolled through the night, because Zeus was planning harm against them.

chapters.title: The Battle on the Plain
paragraphs: When the next morning came, Zeus called the gods to an assembly on the highest ridge of Olympus and spoke to them:

“Listen, gods and goddesses! Let none of you dare to go against my word. Any of you who helps either the Greeks or the Trojans, I will strike with thunder, or else hurl far down into the darkness of Tartarus, whose gates are iron and whose threshold is bronze, and he will learn that I am chief among the gods. And if you want to test my strength, let down a golden chain from heaven to earth, and all of you, gods and goddesses, take hold of it. Still you will not drag Zeus down, however hard you pull. But if I chose to pull with all my strength, I could lift you all up, with the earth and sea as well, tie the chain around a peak of Olympus, and leave you hanging there. That is how much stronger I am than all the rest.”
Tar’-tar-us.

All the gods sat silent and amazed. At last Athene spoke. “Father Zeus, we know well that no one can resist your strength. Yet we pity the Greeks and fear they will be wiped out completely. We will stay out of the war, as you command, but we will give them advice.”

Zeus smiled at her and agreed. Then he harnessed his swift horses to his chariot and touched them with his whip. They flew midway between heaven and earth and reached Ida, the mountain of many springs. There he halted, sat down among the peaks, and looked out over the city of Troy and the Greek army.

The Greeks ate their meal in haste and put on their armor. In the city the Trojans got ready for battle too. They were fewer than their enemies, but just as eager to fight, for they were in desperate need: they had to fight for their wives and children. Then the gates were opened, and the people hurried out.

The two armies met, shield against shield and spear against spear, and the shields clashed with a great ringing noise. As the morning went on, neither side gained the upper hand. But at noon Father Zeus held up his golden scales on high and placed two weights of death in them, one for the Greeks and one for the Trojans. He took the scales by the middle and let them hang, and the Greeks’ side sank lower. Then he sent a blazing thunderbolt from the heights of Ida into the crowd, and when they saw it, they were filled with dismay.

After that, no man could hold his ground. Only Nestor stayed, against his will, because Paris had shot one of his chariot horses with an arrow. While the old man was cutting the harness free, Hector came through the crowd. Nestor would have been killed, but Diomed quickly saw his danger. With a loud shout he called to Ulysses and said:
“Son of Laertes, where are you running, turning your back like a coward? Make sure no one stabs you in the back with a spear. Stop, and help keep this fierce warrior away from old Nestor.”
So he called, but Ulysses paid no attention and ran quickly to the ships.

Then Diomed charged alone into the front line and pulled up beside old Nestor’s chariot. “Old man,” he said, “the young fighters are pressing you hard. Your strength is fading, your charioteer is weak, and your horses are slow. Come up into my chariot and see what the horses I took from Æneas can do—how they can run from danger or chase an enemy, and wheel this way and that! Your charioteer and mine can take care of your horses. Come with me, and Hector will find out whether Diomed’s spear still has any strength in it.”

Nestor agreed. He took the reins in his hand and cracked the whip. They soon drew close to Hector, and Diomed threw his spear. He missed Hector but hit his charioteer in the chest, and the man fell from the chariot while the swift horses shied back. Hector’s heart was heavy with grief for his friend, but he left him lying where he fell, because he had to find another charioteer.

The Trojans would have been routed then and shut up inside their city like sheep in a pen, if Zeus had not hurled a blazing thunderbolt. It fell right in front of Diomed’s chariot. The horses crouched down in fear, and Nestor, badly frightened, let the reins drop from his hands and cried out loud:

“Son of Tydeus, turn your horses and run! Don’t you see that Zeus is not on your side? Today he gives glory to Hector; tomorrow, perhaps, he will give it to you. No one can stand against the will of Zeus.”
The son of Tydeus answered, “Old man, you speak sensibly. But it cuts me to the heart that Hector will say, ‘Diomed ran from me, making for the ships.’ May the earth swallow me up first!”
Nestor replied, “Even if Hector calls you a coward, the Trojans will not believe him, and neither will the daughters of Troy, whose brave husbands you have tumbled in the dust.”

With that he turned the horses and fled. But Hector shouted after Diomed, “Are you the man the Greeks honor with the best seat at the feast and with overflowing cups of wine? They won’t honor you that way anymore. Run, girl! Run, coward! Will you climb our walls and carry off our daughters in your ships?”

Diomed was furious and could not decide whether to run or turn and fight. When he began to turn, Zeus thundered from on high and frightened him. Hector told the Trojan army to take courage, because Zeus was with them, and he called to his horses: “Come now, Bayard, Whitefoot, Flame of Fire, and Brilliant! Remember how well the lovely Andromache has looked after you—even better than she looked after me, her own husband. Carry me fast, so that I can win old Nestor’s shield, which men say is solid gold, and strip from Diomed’s shoulders the breastplate that Hephæstus made.”

The Greeks fled in a rush back inside the wall they had built, with Hector driving them before him, and the whole space between the wall and the ships was jammed with chariots and men. Hector would then have burned the ships, if Hera had not put it into King Agamemnon’s heart to rally the Greeks to battle. He stood on the ship of Ulysses, which lay in the middle of the line, so that his voice could carry to both ends, to where Ajax the Greater had drawn up his ships on one side and Achilles on the other. And he shouted:

“Shame on you, Greeks! What has become of your boasts that each of you could beat a hundred, even two hundred Trojans? Now one single man is worth more than all of you together! Father Zeus, at least let us escape with our lives.”

Zeus heard his prayer and sent a sign from heaven: an eagle carrying a young goat in its claws. It dropped the goat beside the altar of Zeus. When the Greeks saw it, they took heart, leaped at the Trojans, and found joy in the fight again.

Diomed was the first in the charge. After him came the sons of Atreus, both Ajaxes, and all the chiefs, including Teucer, who stood under the shield of Ajax, son of Telamon, as he drew his bow. Ajax would lift his shield a little, and Teucer would peer out and shoot a warrior in the crowd. Then he would duck back like a child to its mother, and Ajax would cover him with the shield. Teucer killed eight men this way. When Agamemnon saw it, he came close and said, “Keep shooting, Teucer, and be a light to your people and to your father Telamon. When Zeus and Athene let me plunder Troy, I will give you a fine reward, the first after my own share.”
Teu’-cer. Tel’-a-mon.
Teucer answered, “I have shot eight arrows, and every one has sunk into a warrior’s flesh. But there is one man I cannot hit.”

He said this and sent another arrow flying from the string, aiming at Hector. He missed Hector but killed a son of Priam. Once more he shot, and this time he killed Hector’s charioteer, hitting him full in the chest as he rushed into battle. Hector’s heart grew dark with rage and grief. He jumped down from his chariot, picked up a stone, and went toward Teucer, meaning to crush him. Teucer took an arrow from his quiver and fitted it to the string, but just as he drew it back to his shoulder, Hector struck him at the place where the collarbone lies between neck and chest. The bowstring snapped, his arm and wrist went numb, the bow flew from his hand, and he fell to one knee. Ajax stood over him and covered him with his shield, and two of his comrades carried him, groaning deeply, to the ships.

Then Zeus again put courage into the Trojans, and they drove the Greeks back to the ditch. Hector stayed always in the front, glorying in his strength. Just as a dog chases a wild boar or a lion and seizes it by the hip or thigh, so Hector clung to the Greeks and struck down the stragglers as they fled.
Hera saw this and felt sorry for them, and she said to Athene, “Shall we not take pity on the Greeks once more? Hector is destroying them.”

Athene answered, “This is all the work of my father, who listened to Thetis when she begged him to give honor to Achilles. But another day, perhaps, he will listen to me. So get the horses ready while I put on my armor for war. We’ll see whether Hector is glad when he sees you and me at the head of the battle.”
So Hera readied the chariot, and Athene put on her armor. When she was armed, Hera whipped up the horses, and the great gates of heaven, which the Hours guard, swung open before them.

But Zeus saw them from Mount Ida and said to Iris of the golden wings, “Go now, swift Iris, and tell these two not to come face to face with me, because our meeting would go badly for them. I will throw them from their chariot and smash it to pieces. If the lightning strikes them, they will not recover from their wounds for ten years.”
So Iris hurried on her way and gave the two goddesses their Father’s message.
Then Hera said to Athene, “We will no longer fight Zeus for the sake of mortal men. Let them live or die as chance decides.”
So the two of them went back to Olympus and sat down in their golden chairs among the other gods, with very heavy hearts.
Zeus also hurried from Ida to Olympus and entered the gods’ assembly. But Hera and Athene sat apart, said nothing, and asked no questions.

Then Zeus said, “Why are you so downcast? Tomorrow will bring worse things than these. Great Hector will not stop his killing until the son of Peleus is roused beside his ships, on the day when they fight over the body of Patroclus.”
Pe’-leus.
Now the sun sank into the sea. The Trojans were angry to see the light go, but the Greeks welcomed the night.
Then Hector called the Trojans to an assembly. In his hand he held a spear eleven cubits long, with a blazing bronze point and a golden ring around it. Leaning on it, he said:
cubit, a foot and a half.

“Listen, Trojans and allies! I thought that today I would destroy the Greek army and their ships and then return to Troy, but night has stopped me. Let us give in to the night and eat our meal. Unharness your horses and feed them. Also bring cattle, sheep, wine, and bread from the city, and plenty of firewood, so that we can keep many fires burning and the Greeks can’t slip away across the sea in the night. Also have the heralds announce in the city that the boys and the old men should guard the wall, that every woman should light a big fire in her house, and that everyone should keep watch, so that no ambush can enter the city while the people are away. In the morning we will arm ourselves, start the war again beside the ships, and bring ruin on the Greeks.”

So Hector spoke, and all the Trojans shouted their approval. They unhitched their horses, brought food from the city, and gathered firewood. All night long they sat in high hope. On some windless night the stars shine bright around the moon, and every crag and valley stands out, and the hilltops too, and the whole depth of the sky lies open, and every star shows, and the shepherd’s heart is glad. In just that way the Trojan fires glittered between the river Xanthus and the ships. A thousand fires were burning, and fifty men sat in the glow of each, while the horses stood beside the chariots, munching their grain and waiting for the dawn.
Xan’-thus (X is pronounced as Z).

chapters.title: The Embassy to Achilles
paragraphs: While the Trojans kept watch in good hope, the Greeks were filled with fear, and King Agamemnon was more troubled than anyone. He told the heralds to call every man to the assembly. They sat down gloomily, and when the King stood up to speak, his tears fell like water running down a steep cliff from a spring that the sun never touches. He said, “Friends, lords and leaders of the Greeks, Zeus has dealt cruelly with me. Once he promised that I would take the city of Troy and then sail home. Now he has deceived me and orders me to go back in disgrace, after losing so many of my people. So let us flee with our ships to the land of our fathers, because we cannot take Troy.”

For a long time the chiefs were silent, for they had lost heart. At last Diomed rose and said, “Do not be angry, O King, if I argue against this madness of yours. You have called me lazy and a coward, and the Greeks, young and old, know well whether I am. Zeus has given you rule and the power of the scepter above your fellows, but he has not given you courage, and courage is the best gift of all. Now if your heart is set on going home, then go. The way is short, and your ships are by the sea. But all the other Greeks will stay until they have taken Troy. And if they too want to leave, then the two of us, I and Sthenelus, will stay and fight until we put an end to the city, because it was the gods who sent us here.”

Then Nestor said, “You are brave in war, son of Tydeus, and better in council than any of your fellows. But now let us eat our meal and post sentries along the trench. And you, son of Atreus, should give a feast for your chiefs, as is right. Whoever gives you the wisest advice, you must follow. We badly need wise counsel, since the enemy has so many fires near our ships. This night will either save our army or destroy it.”

So King Agamemnon invited the chiefs to a feast. When it was over, Nestor stood up and said, “It was a black day, O King, when you sent for the girl Briseis and took her from the tent of Achilles. Let us now think how we can best win him over with noble gifts and kind words.”

King Agamemnon said, “What you say is true, old man. I acted like a fool that day, and I do not deny it. A man whom Zeus loves is worth more than whole armies, and Zeus clearly loves this man, since he is routing the Greeks to do him honor. But as I wronged him in my folly, so I will make amends and pay him more than words can tell. Now I will announce to you all the gifts I will give: a huge treasure of gold and bronze, and twelve strong horses that have won prizes in races by their speed. I will also give him seven women, skilled in fine handiwork and more beautiful than all other women. These I will give him, and with them the girl Briseis, just as I took her from him. And if the gods let us destroy Priam’s great city, he can come when we divide the spoil and choose twenty Trojan women for himself, the most beautiful there are after Helen. And if he comes back to the land of Greece, he will be my son, and he can choose whichever of my daughters he likes in marriage. I will give seven fine cities with her, with pastures and vineyards, where men with many flocks and herds live, who will honor him with gifts as men honor a god and will carry out his commands. All this I will give him, if only he will give up his anger.”

Nestor answered him, “No one could look down on the gifts you offer to great Achilles. So come, let us choose men to go to his tent as quickly as possible. Let Phœnix, who is loved by Zeus, lead the way, and let Ajax the Greater and Ulysses go with him, along with two heralds.”
Phœ’-nix.

So the heralds walked along the seashore, and as they went they prayed to the god who shakes the earth that they might win over the heart of Achilles. When they reached the ships of the Myrmidons, they found the King amusing himself with a harp. He sat there, delighting his soul with music and singing of the deeds of heroes of long ago. Patroclus sat across from him in silence, waiting for him to finish. Then the two chiefs stepped forward, with Ulysses in the lead, and stood before Achilles, who leaped up in great surprise, still holding the harp. Patroclus also rose from his seat when he saw the two men. Then swift-footed Achilles said, “You are welcome, and very dear to me, in spite of all my anger.”

So Achilles spoke and led them forward, and he had them sit on seats covered with purple coverlets. Then he said to Patroclus, “Bring out the biggest bowl and mix a cup for each man, because I have no dearer friends than these who have come under my roof today.

The chiefs reached out for the meat that was laid ready for them. When they had eaten and drunk as much as they wanted, Ajax nodded to Phœnix to start speaking. But Ulysses noticed it and got in ahead of him. He filled a cup with wine, raised it to Achilles, and said: “Your health, Achilles! We have never lacked a good feast, either in King Agamemnon’s tent or now in yours. But today feasting is not on our minds. We can see destruction close at hand, and we are afraid. We honestly doubt that we can save our ships unless you put on your strength again. Today the Trojans and their allies have come right up to the ships to burn them, and Zeus is sending them good signs. Hector rages furiously. He trusts in Zeus, and he swears he will burn the ships and cut the Greeks down while they are dazed by the smoke. In my heart I fear that the god will make his threats come true, and that we will die here in Troy, far from the plains of Argos. So get up, if you are willing, even now, to rescue the Greeks! Do not wait, or you will be sorry later, because there is no cure for what is already done. Give up your anger. Agamemnon is offering you rich gifts: a great treasure of gold and bronze, twelve strong horses that have won him much wealth by their speed, and seven women who are skilled at handiwork and more beautiful than any others. He will give you back Briseis herself, just as he took her from you. All this he will give, and if we capture Priam’s great city, twenty Trojan women, the loveliest after Helen. And when we return to Greece, you will have his daughter as your wife, whichever one you choose, and with her seven cities, all of them near the sea, a land of vineyards and grain fields, whose people will pay you tribute and honor. But if you still hate Agamemnon and his gifts with all your heart, then at least have pity on the other Greeks, who will honor you like a god. And you may kill Hector, too, because in his madness he will come close to you. He believes that not one man among the Greeks can stand up to him.”

Achilles, the swift runner, answered him: “Son of Laertes, I will speak plainly, because I do not want you sitting in front of me trying to coax me, one man one way and another man another. Why do the Greeks have to make war on the Trojans? Why did the sons of Atreus gather this army and lead it to this land? Wasn’t it for the sake of fair-haired Helen? Tell me, are the sons of Atreus the only men in the world who love their wives? Any good man with a sound heart loves his wife and takes care of her, just as I loved mine, even though I won her with my spear. Agamemnon took her from me and cheated me. Let him not try me again. I know him well, and he will not win me over. Let him make plans now with you, Ulysses, and with the other princes of the army, about how to keep the raging fire away from the ships. He has done many things without my help. He has built a wall and dug a ditch around it, wide and deep, and set stakes in the ditch. Yet even with all this he cannot keep Hector away from the ships. When I was fighting in the Greek army, Hector never dared to draw up his men far from the walls. He barely came as far as the Scæan gates and the fig tree. Once he waited for me there to fight man against man, and he barely escaped my spear. But now that I have no wish to fight him, tomorrow I will make a sacrifice to Zeus and all the gods, then load my ships and launch them on the sea. Yes, tomorrow at dawn you can see them, if you care to look, sailing along the Hellespont, with my men rowing eagerly. And if the god who shakes the earth gives me a fair voyage, I will reach the good land of Phthia on the third morning. All the wealth I left behind when I came to Troy is there. From here I will take even more gold and bronze and iron with me, and fine women slaves, my share of the spoils. King Agamemnon will not cheat me again with his lying words. As for his gifts, I scorn them, even if he gives me ten times as much, or twenty times, everything he has now promised. Even if he gave me gifts as countless as the sand of the sea, he would not persuade me, not until he has suffered a bitterness of spirit like mine. And I will not marry his daughter, not even if she were as beautiful as golden Aphrodite and as skilled at handiwork as bright-eyed Athene. Let him choose some more kingly son-in-law from among the Greeks. As for me, if the gods bring me safely home, Peleus will find me a wife. All the wealth that was stored up in the city of Troy in the days of peace, before the Greeks came here, and all the treasure in the temple of Apollo the Archer in the city of Delphi, I count as nothing compared with life. A man can seize cattle and sheep as spoil, and he can buy treasure and horses. But once a man’s life has passed out through his lips, no raiding or buying can win it back. My mother Thetis, the goddess with the silver feet, has told me my fate, and it is a double one. If I stay in this land and fight against the city of Troy, I will never go home again, but my name will live forever. If I go back to my home, my fame will be taken from me, but I will live a long life and not see the grave soon. So I am leaving, and I advise all of you to leave too, because you will never take Troy as you hope. Zeus, who sees everything ahead of time, holds his hand over it, and its people are brave. Now go, and carry this answer back to the princes of the Greeks. But let the old man Phœnix stay with me in my tent tonight, so that he can sail home in my ship tomorrow. He will sail if he wants to, but I will not take him by force.”
Phthi’-a. Pe’-leus.

That was Achilles’ answer. The chiefs sat silent and still, amazed at how fiercely he had spoken. At last the old man Phœnix replied. He spoke with many tears, because he was deeply afraid that the Greek ships would be destroyed: “If you are really set on leaving, and do not care about saving the ships from the raging fire, how can I bear to be left here without you? The old man Peleus made me your teacher, in speaking and in doing. You would go to a feast with no one but me, or eat your meal in the hall with no one but me. I sat you on my knees, cut the tasty bits of meat for you from the dish, and held the wine cup to your lips. Many a tunic of mine you have soaked, spitting wine all over it. I have suffered much for you, and worked hard for you. I had no child of my own, so you became like a son to me, Achilles, to look after me in my need.”

Then Achilles nodded to Patroclus to make up a bed for the old man Phœnix, so that the other two could leave without delay. Ajax, the son of Telamon, said: “Let us go, Ulysses. I think we will get nothing done here today. Let us take the news back, bad as it is, to the men who are waiting for us.”

Achilles said: “My heart swells with anger when I remember how the son of Atreus shamed me in front of everyone, as if I were some worthless stranger. Go and take my message back. I will not rise up for the battle until Hector, killing the Greeks as he goes, reaches the tents of the Myrmidons and surrounds their ships with fire. But when he comes to my tent and my ships, then I think he will be stopped, however eager he is to fight.”
Then Ajax and Ulysses left and told Achilles’ message to King Agamemnon.

chapters.title: The Adventure of Ulysses and Diomed
paragraphs: The other Greek chiefs slept that night, but King Agamemnon could not sleep. His heart was deeply troubled. When he looked toward Troy and saw the many fires and heard the sound of flutes and pipes and the murmur of men, he was astonished. When he looked toward the ships he groaned and tore his hair, thinking of the harm that might come to his people. Then he decided to ask Nestor for advice. So he got up, pulled his tunic around his chest, tied sandals on his feet, threw a tawny lion’s skin over his shoulders, and took a spear in his hand.
Menelaus could not sleep that night either. He got up, wrapped a leopard’s skin around himself, put a bronze cap on his head, took a spear in his hand, and went to look for his brother.

He found him putting on his armor beside his ship, and said: “Why are you arming? Are you going to send someone to spy on what the Trojans are doing? I am afraid no one will agree to go alone, because it is a daring thing to do.”

King Agamemnon answered him: “We need good advice, my brother, if we are to save the army. The mind of Zeus has truly changed, because no man has ever done as much damage in one day as Hector has done to the Greeks. Run to Ajax and Idomeneus and call them to a council, and I will go to Nestor.”

So the chiefs were called together for a council. First they went to the men who were guarding the camp, and found them awake, not sleeping. Like dogs that hear a wild animal in the woods, the guards kept staring toward the plain, listening for the sound of Trojan feet.
Old Nestor was glad to see them. He said: “Keep watch like this, my children, so that we do not fall prey to our enemies.”
Then he hurried across the trench, and the other princes went with him. They sat down in an open space clear of dead bodies, the very place where Hector had turned back from killing the Greeks.
Nestor stood up and said: “Is there a man here who will go among the Trojans and find out what they plan to do? He will win great honor, and gifts.”
Diomed said: “I am ready to go, but I would like someone to go with me. A companion gives comfort and courage, and two minds are better than one for making plans and seeing what is coming.”

Many were willing to go with Diomed. But Agamemnon said: “Choose the best man, Diomed, and do not think about anyone’s birth or rank.” Diomed answered: “If I may choose, who could I choose better than the wise Ulysses? He is brave and sensible, and Athene loves him dearly.”
But Ulysses said: “Do not praise me too much, or blame me. Let us just go, because the night is nearly over.”

So the two men put on their armor. Diomed took a two-edged sword, a shield, and a helmet with no crest. Ulysses took a bow, a quiver, a sword, and a helmet made of hide with the white tusks of a wild boar set around it. Both prayed to Athene to help them, and then they set off through the darkness like two lions, stepping over dead bodies, weapons, and blood.

Meanwhile Hector was thinking along the same lines. He called the chiefs to a council and said: “Who will go and spy among the Greeks, and find out what they plan to do tomorrow, and whether they are keeping watch through the night? He will have a rich reward, a chariot and horses, the best in the whole Greek camp.”
A man named Dolon stood up. He was ugly, but a fast runner. He said:—
Do’-lon.
“I will go, Hector. But come, raise your scepter and swear to me that you will give me the chariot and horses of Achilles.”
So Hector swore it to him. Dolon took his bow, a helmet of gray wolf-skin, and a sharp spear, and set off quickly. But Ulysses saw him, and said:—

“Here comes a man, Diomed, but I cannot tell whether he is a spy or a robber of the dead. Let him pass by a little way so that we can catch him. If he outruns us, drive him with your spear toward the ships, and make sure he does not turn back to the city.”

So they lay down among the dead, a little off the path, and Dolon went past without noticing them. When he had gone a short distance, they ran after him. For a moment he stood listening to their steps, because he thought Hector had sent friends to call him back. But when they were a spear’s throw from him, or less, he saw they were enemies and ran. Like two hounds chasing a fawn or a hare, they raced after Dolon. And when he had almost reached the trench, with the two of them keeping him from turning back to the city, Diomed rushed forward and shouted:—
“Stop, or I will kill you with my spear.”

He threw the spear, but he made it fly over Dolon’s shoulder, so that it stuck in the ground in front of him. Dolon stood there trembling and pale, with his teeth chattering in fear. The two heroes came up, breathing hard, and grabbed him. Weeping, he said:—
“Hold me for ransom. My father will give you plenty of gold and bronze and iron if he hears that I am a prisoner at the ships.”

The wise Ulysses said: “Tell us the truth. Why were you coming this way through the darkness? To rob the dead? Or to spy on our affairs at the ships, on Hector’s orders? Or on some errand of your own?”

Dolon answered: “Hector talked me into it. He promised to give me the horses and chariot of Achilles, and he told me to go and spy out what you planned to do tomorrow, and whether you were keeping watch during the night.”
Ulysses smiled and said: “That was certainly a big reward your heart was set on. But tell me, where is Hector, and where are the Trojan guards?”

Dolon answered: “Hector is holding a council with the chiefs. As for the army, no guards are set, except where the Trojans themselves are camped. The allies sleep without worry and count on the Trojans to watch for them, since they have no wives or children nearby.”
Ulysses asked: “Do they sleep mixed in with the Trojans, or apart from them?”

“Next to the sea,” said Dolon. “But if you want to get into the camp, look: off by themselves are some newcomers, the Thracians, with Rhesus their king. I have never seen horses so beautiful and tall as his. They are whiter than snow and faster than the winds. But now, either send me to the ships, or, if you like, tie me up and leave me here.”
Thra’-ci-ans. Rhe’-sus.

But Diomed answered: “Don’t imagine you’ll get away, Dolon, even though your news is good. If I let you go, you’d only come back to spy on our camp or to fight us. Once I kill you, you’ll never trouble the Greeks again.”

With that he killed him and stripped off his armor. He hung it on a tamarisk tree and marked the spot with reeds and tamarisk branches, so they could find it on their way back. Then the two went on across the plain until they reached the Thracians, who lay asleep. Each man’s weapons were laid out neatly beside him, along with his horses. In the middle lay King Rhesus, his horses tied to the rail of his chariot. Now Diomed began the killing. He fell on the Thracians the way a lion falls on a flock of sheep. He killed twelve of them, and as each one fell Ulysses dragged the body aside, to clear a path for the horses. He was afraid they would shy away from the dead, since they were not used to war. The thirteenth man was King Rhesus himself, who lay gasping in his sleep, because an evil dream was pressing on him. Meanwhile Ulysses led the horses out of the camp, striking them with his bow, since he hadn’t thought to take the whip from the chariot. Then he whistled as a signal for Diomed to come. But Diomed was hanging back, wondering whether he could kill even more. Then Athene whispered in his ear:—
“Think about getting back safely, or some god may stir the Trojans up against you.”

In fact, Apollo was already stirring them up, and the Trojans were gathering in a noisy, shouting crowd. But by then Diomed and Ulysses had mounted the horses and were riding for the ships. Their friends were glad to see them back safe, and praised them warmly for everything they had done.

chapters.title: The Wounding of the Chiefs
paragraphs: When the next day dawned, King Agamemnon called the Greeks to battle, and on the other side Hector drew up the men of Troy in order. Like an ominous star that shines out from the clouds and then disappears again, Hector was seen now among the front ranks and now giving orders to the rear.

Then the Trojans and the Greeks hurled themselves at each other. As reapers work across a rich man’s field, cutting the barley and wheat down in long rows, so the Trojans and the Greeks cut each other down. All morning, while the day was growing, the battle stayed even, and men fell equally on both sides. But at noon the Greeks broke through the Trojan line, with Agamemnon the first man into the gap. As fire falls on a forest and sweeps it away, so Agamemnon fell on the Trojans and swept them before him. They fled past the Tomb of Ilus and past the wild fig tree in the plain, with the King close behind them, shouting loudly. But when they reached the Scæan gate they turned and made a stand, and the fighting started again.
I’-lus.

Then Zeus spoke to Iris. “Go quickly, swift Iris,” he said, “and carry this message to Hector. As long as he sees King Agamemnon cutting down the ranks of men, he must keep out of the fight. But when the King is wounded by a spear or an arrow and jumps down from his chariot, then Hector may go forward. I will give him strength to keep killing until he reaches the ships and the sun goes down.”

So Iris went and gave these words to Hector. When Hector heard them, he jumped down from his chariot and went up and down the Trojan ranks, encouraging the men for the fight. Then the two armies stood and faced each other.

Then King Agamemnon killed the two sons of Antenor. First he killed Iphidamas, striking him a deadly blow on the neck. But Coön, Antenor’s eldest son, was full of grief for his brother. Standing off to one side, where the King could not see him, he stabbed Agamemnon in the arm below the elbow, and the spear went right through. The King flinched, but he did not stop fighting. Coön was dragging his brother out of the crowd by the foot and calling on the chiefs to help. Then Agamemnon struck him with his spear under the shield and brought him to the ground, and cut off his head with his sword. That was how Agamemnon killed the two sons of Antenor.
I-phid’-a-mas. Co’-on.

For a while, as long as the wound was still warm, the King kept fighting as before. But when it turned cold and stiff, terrible pain came over him. He jumped into his chariot and ordered the charioteer to drive him to the ships, because he could fight no longer.

When Hector saw that Agamemnon had left the battle, he called out to the Trojans and their allies: “Come on, show yourselves men! The leader of the Greeks is gone, and Zeus is giving the glory to me.”

So he stirred up their spirits. Like a hunter setting his dogs on a wild boar or a lion in the open, Hector set the Trojans on the Greeks. He went among the foremost himself and plunged into the fight like a storm breaking over the sea. He killed many brave men, until Ulysses called out to Diomed: “Son of Tydeus, have we forgotten how to be brave? Come over here and stand by me. It would be a disgrace if Hector took our ships.”
Strong Diomed answered, “I will stay with you, certainly. But it will go badly for us if Zeus gives the victory to the Trojans instead of to us.”

With that he killed a man, and Ulysses killed another. After that they killed two men each, holding their ground against the Trojans, and the Greeks, who had been running from Hector, gladly caught their breath and turned back to fight.

Hector was quick to see what they were doing. He charged at them with a shout, and the Trojan companies followed him. When Diomed saw him, he was afraid, and he said to Ulysses, “Look, mighty Hector is coming at us. Let’s stand firm and face him.”

And as he spoke he threw his spear, and his aim was true. It struck Hector on the helmet, but it glanced off the bronze without wounding his flesh, because the helmet Apollo had given him saved him. Still, Hector reeled under the blow and fell to one knee, and darkness came over his eyes. Diomed went after his spear, which had flown far through the front ranks and landed on the ground. While he was gone, Hector got his breath back, jumped into his chariot, and drove into the middle of his army, escaping death.

Then Diomed, rushing forward with his spear in his hand, shouted: “Dog! You’ve escaped death once more, but it was a close thing. Apollo saved you, no doubt, and you must have prayed to him before you entered the fight. But I will kill you someday, if only some god will help me.”

Then he turned to kill more Trojans. But Paris was hiding behind the pillar on the Tomb of Ilus. He drew his bow and shot Diomed through the ankle of his right foot. Then he boasted loudly of his aim. “I only wish,” he said, “that I had hit you in the side. Then you would never trouble the sons of Troy again.”

But Diomed answered: “Your bow won’t do you much good, you cowardly archer, if you ever dare to face me man to man. As for this scratch on my foot, I care about it no more than if a woman or a child had hit me. The wounds I give are not like that.”

Then Ulysses stood in front of him while he pulled the arrow out of his foot. The wound hurt terribly, for all his brave words. So he jumped into his chariot and told the driver to hurry to the ships. Ulysses was left standing alone, with none of the Greeks beside him, because they were all badly frightened. Then he spoke to himself:—

“What am I to do? It would be a great disgrace to run from all these enemies, but it would be worse to be caught and killed, because Zeus has clearly filled the Greeks with fear. But why am I talking this way? Only a coward pulls back from the war. A brave man holds his ground, whether he strikes or is struck.”

As he spoke, the Trojans closed in around him, like men with dogs closing in on a wild boar that stands at bay, gnashing his white tusks. Ulysses stood at bay fiercely, and killed five famous chiefs. But before one of them fell, he wounded Ulysses in the side and scraped the flesh from his ribs. Blood spurted high from the wound, and the Trojans shouted when they saw it. Then Ulysses cried out for help. He shouted three times, and Menelaus heard him and called to Ajax, saying:—
“Ajax, I hear the voice of Ulysses! He is shouting as if the Trojans had surrounded him and left him all alone. Come, let’s help him before he comes to harm, or the Greeks will suffer a heavy loss!”

With these words he led the way, and Ajax followed. When they reached Ulysses, the Trojans were crowding around him, like jackals around a long-horned stag in the hills that a hunter has wounded with an arrow. The stag runs from the hunter while the wound is still warm, but when he grows weak the jackals tear him apart. Then a lion comes, and the jackals run. In the same way the Trojans ran when Ajax arrived and stood beside Ulysses. Then Menelaus took Ulysses by the hand and led him out of the crowd.

Then Ajax charged at the Trojans and killed many of them, sweeping across the plain and cutting down horse and man alike. But Paris, the husband of Helen, kept Machaon out of the fight by wounding him in the right shoulder with a three-pointed arrow. So Idomeneus said to Nestor, “Quick, Nestor, get into your chariot and take Machaon with you, and drive fast to the ships. One physician is worth as much as many other men!”
So Nestor climbed into his chariot, and Machaon stood beside him. He touched the horses, and they flew eagerly to the ships.

Now Achilles was standing on the stern of his ship, watching the battle, and he saw Nestor carrying Machaon in his chariot toward the ships. He called to Patroclus, who was in the tent, and Patroclus came out. Then Achilles said:—

“Soon the Greeks will be coming to beg me for help, because they are in terrible need. But go and find out who it is that Nestor is taking to the ships. The shoulders look like Machaon’s, but I didn’t see his face, because the horses went by so fast.”
Then Patroclus ran to Nestor’s tent and stood in the doorway. When old Nestor saw him, he came and took him by the hand and tried to make him sit down. But Patroclus refused, saying:—

“Don’t keep me. I only came to see who it is you’ve brought wounded from the battle, and now I see that it is Machaon. So I’ll go back, because you know what kind of man Achilles is, how hasty he is and how quick to blame.”

Then Nestor said: “But why should Achilles care about the Greeks? Why does he ask who is wounded? Listen to what I say. Maybe Achilles will not go out to the battle. But let him send you out, with the Myrmidons behind you, and let him put his own armor on you. Then the Trojans will be terrified, thinking he has joined the fight, and we will get a chance to catch our breath.”
Then Patroclus went back to Achilles.

chapters.title: The Battle at the Wall
paragraphs: By this time the Trojans had come up close to the trench. But the horses stopped at the edge, afraid to jump it, because it was wide and deep, and the Greeks had set great stakes in it. Then Polydamas spoke.
Po-lyd’-a-mas.

“Hector, it is madness to try to cross the trench in our chariots. It is wide and deep, and there are great stakes in it. And think about this too: even if we did manage to cross, how would things stand? If Zeus really wants the Greeks to be wiped out completely, then all will be well. But if they turn on us and chase us back from the ships, we won’t be able to retreat. So let’s leave our chariots here at the edge and go on foot against the wall.”

So they went forward in five companies, and Hector led the one that was bravest and largest. In each company the men locked their shields together and so advanced on the Greeks. They all left their chariots by the trench, except Asius alone. Asius drove his chariot right up to the gate on the left side of the wall. As it happened, the gates were open, because the guards had opened them so that any fleeing Greeks could get in. The guards were two mighty heroes, and when they saw Asius and his company coming, they went outside and stood in front of the gates, like two wild boars standing at bay against a crowd of men and dogs. All the while the men on the wall threw down heavy stones, which fell on the Trojans as thick as snowflakes in winter, and the helmets and shields rang loudly. Many Trojans fell wounded to death, and for all his fury Asius could not force his way in. But at another gate, where Hector was leading, a strange marvel appeared in the sky. An eagle was carrying a great snake in its claws, which it had caught as prey. But the snake fought fiercely for its life and twisted around until it bit the eagle on the breast. The eagle dropped it into the middle of the army and flew away with a loud cry. Then Polydamas, the wise counselor, came up to Hector and said:—
A’-si-us.

“We should not follow these Greeks to their ships. I think the marvel we have just seen is a sign for us. The eagle caught a snake in its claws but could not keep hold of it, and dropped it before it could carry it to its young. The same will happen to us. We will drive the Greeks back to their ships, but we will not defeat them, and we will come back in disorder the way we came, leaving many of our comrades behind us.”

But Hector frowned and answered: “No, that is bad advice, Polydamas. Are you telling me to forget the command of Zeus the Thunderer and pay attention to birds and how they fly? I don’t care whether they go east or west, right or left. A brave man needs only one sign: that he is fighting for his country. So be careful, because if you hold back from the war, or hold anyone else back, I swear I will strike you down with my spear.”

Then Hector sprang forward, and the Trojans charged after him with a shout. Zeus sent a great blast of wind down from Mount Ida, and it carried the dust of the plain straight toward the ships and troubled the hearts of the Greeks. The Trojans began to tear the battlements off the wall and to pull up the posts that had been set in to strengthen it. But the Greeks did not give ground. They locked their shields together and fought to hold the wall, and the two Ajaxes, the Greater and the Less, stood at the front. Snow falls thick in the middle of winter, when the winds are still and it covers the mountaintops, the plains, the houses of men, and even the seashore right down to the edge of the waves. In just that way the stones came down, thrown by the Greeks from the wall at the Trojans, and thrown back again by the Trojans at the Greeks. Still Hector and his men could not break through the gate. But at last Zeus stirred up his own son Sarpedon. Sarpedon advanced with his shield held in front of him and a spear shaking in each hand. A lion, pressed by hunger, will attack a pen of oxen or a sheepfold, and it does not care if it finds men and dogs on guard against it. Sarpedon went against the wall in the same way.

On the other side, the Greeks closed their ranks along the wall, because this fight meant life or death. For a long time the two sides were evenly matched. The Lycians could not break through the Greek wall and open a path to the ships, and the Greeks could not drive the Lycians away from it. Two neighbors stand with measuring rods in their hands and argue over where a boundary should run. The Lycians and the Greeks argued over the battlements in the same way. Many men were cut down by the merciless bronze, some struck in the back where they had no protection, some struck in front, right through their shields. The blood of men spattered all the battlements.
It went on like this until Zeus gave the glory to Hector. Hector leapt inside the wall and shouted to the Trojans, “Follow me now! Tear down the wall and burn the ships!”

At his words the Trojans heard him and rushed together at the wall. In front of the gate lay a huge stone, broad at the bottom and sharp at the top. Two of the strongest men alive today could hardly have lifted it with levers onto a wagon. Hector picked it up with ease, as easily as a shepherd carries a sheep’s fleece in one hand. The gates had two folding doors, held shut by bolts and a key. Hector planted his feet wide apart, so that his throw would be steadier and stronger, and hurled the great stone at them. It struck the gates with a tremendous crash. The bolts could not hold against it, the hinges snapped, and the doors flew open. Then Hector leapt into the gap with a spear in each hand, his eyes blazing like fire. The Trojans came after him, some climbing over the wall and some pouring through the gates.

chapters.title: The Battle at the Ships
paragraphs: Once Zeus had brought the Trojans close to the ships, he turned his eyes away and watched them no longer. He believed that none of the immortal gods would come to help either the Trojans or the Greeks. But Poseidon was watching the battle from the wooded peak of Samothrace, where he could see Ida, Troy, and the ships. He pitied the Greeks when he saw them running from Hector, and he made up his mind to help them. He left the peak of Samothrace and reached his palace in the depths of the sea in four strides. There he harnessed his horses to his chariot and drove out over the waves. The great creatures of the sea leapt and played around him as he went, because they knew their king.
Po-sei’-don. Sa-mo-thrace’.
He stabled his horses in a cave under the sea, unhitched them from the chariot, gave them immortal food to eat, and fastened golden shackles around their feet.
All the while the Trojans were advancing behind Hector like a storm or a roaring fire, because they meant to capture the ships and kill the Greeks beside them.

Poseidon went to the Greek camp, taking the shape of Calchas the herald. He spoke first to the two Ajaxes. “Stand firm, you mighty men, and you will save the army,” he said. “I am not afraid for the rest of the wall, only for the place where Hector is raging.”
Cal’-chas.
As he spoke, he struck each of them with his staff. He filled them with courage and gave strength to their hands and feet. Then he left them, as swiftly as a hawk rising from a cliff to chase a bird.

The Lesser Ajax recognized him and said to his companion, “That was some god telling us to fight for the ships. It was not Calchas, because I noticed how his legs and feet moved as he walked away. Gods are easy to recognize. And my heart is certainly eager for the fight now.”

The Greater Ajax answered him, “I feel the same way. My hands are itching to grip my spear, my heart is on fire, and my feet are carrying me forward. I am eager to face Hector, even alone, for all his fury.”
Then Poseidon went to the other chiefs. He moved up and down the ranks and urged them to stand firm against their enemies. But the Trojans pressed on just the same, with Hector leading the way.

The cry of battle was so loud that it reached old Nestor, who was sitting in his tent and caring for the wounded Machaon. He went out to look for King Agamemnon. On the way, the king met him, and with him were Diomed and Ulysses, who had also been wounded that day. The leaders met to talk things over. Agamemnon was deeply troubled that so many of his people were being killed, and he wanted to haul the ships down into the sea and sail for home as soon as darkness fell and the Trojans stopped fighting.

But Ulysses would not hear of it. “Son of Atreus,” he said, “you are surely not fit to rule over us, who have been soldiers since we were young. Will you abandon this city, when we have suffered so much to take it? That cannot be. Let no Greek hear you say such things. And what is this talk of launching our ships now, while the armies are in the middle of a fight? If we did that, we would all die together. The Greeks would stop fighting when they saw the ships being launched, and the Trojans would kill every one of us.”

King Agamemnon replied, “You are right.” He went through the army and told the men to fight bravely. All this time Poseidon was putting courage and strength into their hearts. On the other side, Hera put Zeus to sleep on the heights of Olympus, so that the battle now turned against the Trojans.

Ajax picked up a huge stone, one of the many that were lying about as props for the ships, and struck Hector on the neck, just above the rim of his shield. Hector fell like an oak struck down by the thunderbolt of Zeus. The Greeks rushed forward with a great shout to drag him away, but they could not, because all the bravest Trojans held their shields over him. They carried him to the river and poured water over him. After a while he sat up, and then he passed out again, because the blow had been a terrible one. When the Greeks saw that Hector had been carried out of the battle, they pressed forward harder, killing Trojans and driving them out of the camp and back across the trench. But when the Trojans reached their chariots, which they had left on the far side of the trench, they stopped there, pale and shaking with fear, like men running from a battle.

Now Zeus woke from his sleep and looked down at the earth. He saw the Greeks driving the Trojans back and Hector lying on the plain, vomiting blood, with his friends kneeling around him. Hector lay senseless, because the hand that struck him had been no weak one. Zeus was furious at the sight. He said to Hera, “What have you done, sending Hector out of the battle? Do you not remember how I hung you in the clouds, with a gold chain around your wrists and a gold anvil tied to each foot? Stop your tricks, or nothing will protect you from my anger.”
Hera answered, “It is Poseidon who is hurting the Trojans and helping the Greeks.”

Then Zeus said, “Call Iris and Apollo the Archer here. Let Iris go to Poseidon and tell him to stop fighting. Let Apollo give Hector strength, so that he can go back to the battle. In this way my will shall be done, and I will keep the oath I swore to Thetis of the sea, that I would honor her son.”

Iris went to Poseidon and gave him the message from Zeus. The god was furious. “Does he think he can control me by force, when I am his equal in honor?” he said. “We are three brothers. The Fates gave the sea to me to rule, the realm of darkness to Hades, and the heavens to Zeus. The earth belongs to all of us. I do not live by the will of Zeus. Let him stay in his own possessions and not interfere.”
But Iris answered, “Shaker of the earth, shall I really carry back so rough an answer to Zeus? Surely you know how powerful the elder brother is?”

Poseidon said, “Iris, you speak well. This time I will give way. But know this: if he scorns me and the other gods, leaves Troy standing, and does not give the Greeks victory, there will be endless feuding between him and me.”

Meanwhile Apollo went to Hector, as Zeus had ordered. He found Hector sitting up, since the will of Zeus had revived him. Apollo said, “Hector, why are you sitting here apart from your companions? Has some trouble come to you?”

Hector answered in a weak voice, “Which of the gods are you, to be speaking to me? Do you not know that Ajax struck me with a huge stone and knocked me out of the battle? I truly thought I had gone down to the house of the dead today.”

But Apollo said, “Take heart. Zeus has sent me, Apollo of the Golden Sword, to stand beside you and help you. Come, tell your people to advance toward the ships. I will go ahead of you and make the way easy for your horses.”

So Hector rose up in his strength and rejoined the battle. Like hunters chasing a stag or a wild goat when a lion suddenly crosses their path, the Greeks were afraid when they saw Hector, the son of Priam. One of them said:

“This is a great wonder that I see with my own eyes. We thought Hector had been killed by the hand of Ajax, son of Telamon, and now he has come back to the battle! Many Greeks have already fallen before him, and many more will fall, I think, because some god has surely raised him up and is helping him. Come on, let all the bravest of us stand together. Then, mighty as he is, he will be afraid to break into our ranks.”

All the bravest gathered and stood at the front, while the crowd of soldiers made for the ships. But Hector came on, with Apollo going before him, and many Greeks fell dead before the Trojans. So the battle turned again and came near the trench. Apollo now made the crossing easy for the Trojans, so that they did not leave their chariots at the edge, as before, but drove them across.

The Trojans kept coming, and the Greeks kept giving way. So they reached the ships again, one side pushing forward and the other yielding ground. Hector caught hold of one of the ships, and the battle raged around it. The Trojans and the Greeks crowded around, and nobody fought from a distance with arrows or javelins. They fought man to man, with battle-axes, swords, and great spears pointed at both ends. Many fine weapons lay shattered on the ground, and the earth ran with blood like a river. Still Hector kept his hand on the ship’s prow and shouted to the Trojans to bring fire, because Zeus had given them the victory that day. Even Ajax had to give way then, so hard did the Trojan spears press him. He no longer stood on the stern deck but on the rowers’ bench, and from there he thrust his spear at anyone who tried to set the ship on fire. All the while he shouted to the Greeks in a terrible voice:

“Greeks! Now you must fight like men. Do you have any helpers behind you? Do you have any walls to shelter you? We are here on the plain of Troy, the sea is right behind us, and we are far from our own country. All our hope lies in courage, not in shrinking back from the battle.”
And he kept thrusting with his spear whenever a Trojan, at Hector’s command, tried to bring fire against the ships. He wounded a full twelve of them as he stood there.

chapters.title: The Deeds and Death of Patroclus
paragraphs: Patroclus was standing beside Achilles, weeping bitterly. Achilles said, “What is wrong, Patroclus, that you weep like a little girl who runs along beside her mother, holding her dress and wanting to be picked up, and looks at her with tearful eyes until she lifts her in her arms? Have you heard bad news from home? Or are you weeping for the Greeks, because they are dying for their own foolishness?”

Patroclus said, “Do not be angry with me, great Achilles. The Greeks are in terrible trouble, all their bravest men are wounded, and still you hold on to your anger. If you will not go to the battle because you fear some warning from the gods, then let me go, and let your Myrmidons go with me. Let me put on your armor, so that the Greeks can have a breathing space from the war.”
So he pleaded, not knowing that he was pleading for his own death. And Achilles answered:

“It is no warning that keeps me out of the war. These men took away my prize, which I won with my own hands. But let the past be past. I said I would not rise up until the battle came close to my own ships. But you may put on my armor and lead my Myrmidons into the fight. The Trojans have gathered around the ships like a dark cloud, and the Greeks have hardly any ground to stand on between the Trojans and the sea. They cannot see the gleam of my helmet, Diomed is not there with his spear, and I do not hear the voice of Agamemnon, only the voice of Hector calling the Trojans to battle. So go, Patroclus, and drive the fire away from the ships. Then come back, and do not fight the Trojans any further, or you will take my glory from me. And in the joy of battle, do not go near the walls of Troy, or one of the gods may meet you and hurt you. The keen-archer Apollo loves the Trojans well.”

While they were still talking, Ajax could hold out no longer. Swords and javelins came at him thick and fast and rattled off his helmet. His shoulder ached from the weight of the great shield, he was gasping for breath, and big drops of sweat ran down and fell to the ground. Then Hector came up close and struck his spear with a great sword, and the spearhead dropped off. Ajax was badly frightened and gave ground, and the Trojans set torches to the prow of the ship, so that a huge flame leaped up toward the sky. Achilles saw it, slapped his thigh, and said:
“Hurry, Patroclus! I can see fire rising from the ships. Put on my armor, and I will call my men to the fight.”

So Patroclus put on the armor: the breastplate, the shield, and the helmet. He fastened the silver-studded sword over his shoulder and took a heavy spear in his hand. But he left behind the great spear of Achilles, because no one but Achilles could handle it. Then Automedon harnessed the horses to the chariot, Bayard and Piebald, with Pedasus beside them in the side harness. The first two were immortal horses, but the third was mortal.
Au-tom’-e-don. Ped’-a-sus.
Meanwhile Achilles had called the Myrmidons to battle. He had brought fifty ships to Troy, and each one carried fifty men.

Then Achilles said: “Myrmidons, do not forget the bold things you said against the men of Troy while I was angry. You complained that I was keeping you from the fight against your will. Well, now you have what you wanted.”

So the Myrmidons marched into battle in tight ranks, helmet against helmet and shield against shield, as close together as the stones a builder fits into a wall. In front went Patroclus, with Automedon beside him in the chariot. Then Achilles went into his tent and took a great cup out of his chest, a cup his mother Thetis had given him. No one but Achilles ever drank from that cup, and he poured offerings from it to no god except Zeus. First he cleaned it with sulphur, and then with water from the spring. After that he washed his hands, went and stood in the open space in front of his tent, and poured an offering from the cup to Zeus, saying: “O Zeus, I am sending my comrade into this battle. Make him strong and bold, give him glory, and bring him safely home to the ships, and my men with him.”
That was his prayer. Father Zeus heard him, and granted one part of it and refused the other.

By now Patroclus and the Myrmidons had reached the place where the fighting was fiercest around the ships. When the Trojans saw him, they thought Achilles had given up his anger and come out to the war. They turned and ran, and many famous chiefs fell to Greek spears. The battle rolled back as far as the trench, and in the trench many Trojan chariots were smashed, though the horses of Achilles cleared it in a single stride, so quick and strong were they. Patroclus was determined to kill Hector, but his horses were too fast and he could not catch him. So Patroclus wheeled his chariot around and cut off the men who were running away, then charged back and forth, killing as he went.

But when Sarpedon saw the Lycians scattered and afraid, he called out to them to take courage, and said he would test this great warrior himself. He leaped down from his chariot, and Patroclus leaped down too, and they rushed at each other like two eagles. Sarpedon had a spear in each hand. With one he struck the horse Pedasus, the mortal one, in the right shoulder; with the other he missed, and it flew over Patroclus’s left shoulder. But Patroclus did not miss. He drove his spear into Sarpedon’s heart, and the great Lycian chief fell like an oak, or a poplar, or a pine that is cut down on the hills by the ax. As he fell he called to his companion Glaucus: “Now you must show yourself a good warrior, Glaucus. First rally the men of Lycia to fight for me, and fight yourself as well, because it would be a shame to you for the rest of your days if the Greeks stripped me of my armor.”

With a great shout the Lycians and Trojans charged and pushed the Greeks back a short way from the body, and then the Greeks did the same to them. So the battle went on, until no one could have recognized the great Sarpedon, he was so covered with spears and blood and dust. At last, though, the Greeks drove the Trojans away from the body and stripped off the armor, but they did not harm the body itself. At the command of Zeus, Apollo came down and carried it out of the middle of the fight. He washed it with water, rubbed it with ambrosia, and wrapped it in the clothes of the gods. Then he gave it to Sleep and Death, and these two carried it to Lycia, Sarpedon’s homeland.

Then Patroclus forgot what Achilles had told him, that he must not go near Troy. He chased the Trojans all the way to the city, right up to the wall. Three times he climbed onto the corner of the wall, and three times Apollo himself pushed him back with his shining shield. But the fourth time the god said: “Go back, Patroclus. It is not for you to capture the city of Troy. It is not even for Achilles, and he is far better than you.”

So Patroclus drew back, afraid of the anger of the archer god. Then Apollo put fresh spirit into Hector and sent him against Patroclus. Hector drove out in his chariot, with his brother Cebriones as driver. But when they came near, Patroclus threw a great stone that he was holding and hit Cebriones on the forehead, crushing it in, so that he tumbled headfirst out of the chariot. Patroclus mocked him, saying:
Ceb-ri’-o-nes.
“What an acrobat! Look how smoothly he dives! Think how many oysters he could gather, diving off a ship even in a stormy sea! Who would have guessed there were such fine divers in Troy!”

Then the battle grew hot again around the body of Cebriones, and in the end the Greeks dragged this body away too and stripped off the armor. After that, Patroclus charged at the Trojans again. Three times he charged, and each time he killed nine famous chiefs. But on the fourth charge Apollo stood behind him and struck him on the head and shoulders, so that his eyes went dark. The helmet fell from his head and the horsehair plumes were soiled with dust. It had never touched the ground before, because it was the helmet of Achilles. The god also broke the spear in his hand, knocked the shield from his arm, and loosened his breastplate. Patroclus stood there stunned, and Euphorbus struck him in the back with a spear, but did not kill him. Patroclus tried to escape to the ranks of his comrades. But Hector saw him, thrust at him with his spear, and struck him in the groin, so that he fell. When the Greeks saw him go down, they let out a terrible cry. Then Hector stood over him and said:

“Did you think you would sack our city, Patroclus, and carry off our wives and daughters in your ships? Look! I have killed you, and the birds of the air will eat your flesh. The great Achilles cannot help you at all, the same Achilles who told you to strip the tunic from my chest, and you were fool enough to think you could do it.”
Eu-phor’-bus.

But Patroclus answered: “You boast a lot, Hector. Yet it was not you who killed me but Apollo, who took my armor from me. If twenty men like you had met me, I would have killed every one. And remember this: death and fate are close behind you, and they will come by the hand of the great Achilles.”
Hector replied, though Patroclus was already dead: “Why do you prophesy my death? Maybe the great Achilles himself will fall by my hand.”
Then he pulled his spear out of the wound and went after Automedon to kill him, but the swift horses of Achilles carried Automedon away.

chapters.title: The Rousing of Achilles
paragraphs: The fight over the body of Patroclus was fierce, and many heroes fell on both sides, the first of them Euphorbus, who had wounded Patroclus first. As he came close to strip the dead man of his armor, Menelaus killed him with a spear. Menelaus killed him but did not take his armor, because Hector was coming through the battle, and Menelaus did not dare wait for him. He drew back into the ranks of his own men. Then Hector stripped Patroclus of the armor that the great Achilles had given him to wear. Next he seized the body and would have dragged it into the Trojan army, but Ajax Telamon came forward and held his broad shield over it, the way a lion stands over its cubs when hunters meet it in the woods, and pulls its shaggy brows down over its eyes. Hector gave way, but Glaucus saw it and said:

“You should be ashamed, Hector, that you dare not stand up to Ajax. How will you and your countrymen save the city of Troy? Your allies surely won’t fight for it any longer. They get little good from you. Didn’t Sarpedon fall, and didn’t you leave him as food for the dogs? And now, if you had held your ground and carried off Patroclus, we could have made an exchange and won back Sarpedon and his armor from the Greeks. But that can’t happen, because you are afraid of Ajax and run from him.”
But Hector said: “I am not afraid of him, or of any man. It is only that Zeus gives victory now to one man and now to another. But wait here, and see whether I am a coward, as you say.”

He had already sent the armor of Patroclus to the city. Now he ran after the men who were carrying it, caught up with them, and put the armor on himself (Zeus saw him do it and did not like it). Then he came back to the battle, and everyone who saw him thought he was the great Achilles himself. They all charged together, and the fighting grew fiercer and fiercer as the day went on. The Greeks said to one another: “Better for the earth to open and swallow us alive than to let the Trojans carry Patroclus off to their city.” And the Trojans said: “If we all must fall beside this man, so be it, but we will not give way.” Meanwhile the horses of Achilles stood apart from the battle. They had understood that Patroclus was dead, and they wept. Automedon could not move them with the whip, or with gentle words, or with threats. They would not go back to the ships, and they would not go into the battle. They stood as still as a pillar on a dead man’s tomb, with their heads hanging to the ground, big tears dropping to the earth, and their long manes trailing in the dust.
But Father Zeus saw them and felt sorry for them, and said:

“It was not right to give you, immortal as you are, to a mortal man. Of all the creatures that move on the earth, mortal man has the most sorrow. But Hector will not have you. It is enough for him, more than enough, that he has the armor of Achilles.”

Then the horses moved from their place and obeyed their drivers as before. Hector could not capture them, though he wanted them badly. All the while the battle raged around the dead Patroclus. At last Ajax said to Menelaus (these two had fought more bravely than all the others):
“See if you can find Antilochus, Nestor’s son, so that he can carry the news to Achilles that Patroclus is dead.”
An-til’-o-chus.

So Menelaus went and found Antilochus on the left side of the battle, and said to him: “I have bad news for you. You can see that the men of Troy are winning today. And Patroclus lies dead. Run to Achilles and tell him, in case he can still save the body. As for the armor, Hector has it already.”

Antilochus was horrified to hear this. His eyes filled with tears, and his voice stuck in his throat. Still, he listened to what Menelaus had said and ran off to tell Achilles what had happened. Menelaus went back to Ajax, whom he had left beside Patroclus, and said:

“Antilochus is indeed taking the news to Achilles. But I doubt that Achilles will come, angry as he is with Hector, since he has no armor to protect him. So let us think how best to carry Patroclus away from the men of Troy.”
Then Ajax said: “You and Meriones run forward and lift the body in your arms, and Ajax the Less and I will keep the Trojans off in the meantime.”
Me-ri’-o-nes.

So Menelaus and Meriones ran forward and lifted the body. When the Trojans saw them, they rushed forward with a great shout, like dogs running and barking ahead of the hunters who chase a wild boar. But when the beast turns at bay, the dogs scatter this way and that. In just that way the Trojans fled when Ajax the Greater and Ajax the Less turned to fight. Still, the Greeks kept giving ground and the Trojans kept coming on, and always in front were Hector, the son of Priam, and Æneas, the son of Anchises. In the meantime Antilochus came to Achilles, who had seen the Greeks running and the Trojans chasing them and was already badly afraid. Antilochus spoke to him, weeping as he did so:
An-chi’-ses.
“I bring bad news. Patroclus lies dead. The Greeks are fighting over his body, but Hector has his armor.”

Then Achilles scooped up dust from the ground in his hand and poured it over his head, threw himself full length on the ground, and tore his hair. All the women wailed. Antilochus sat there weeping, but he kept hold of Achilles’s hands the whole time, so that Achilles would not kill himself in his great grief.
Then his mother heard his cry, where she sat in the depths of the sea, and came to him, laid her hand on him, and said:
“Why are you weeping, my son? Do not hide it from me. Tell me.”

And Achilles answered: “Everything that Zeus promised you for my sake he has done. But what good is it to me, when my friend Patroclus is dead and Hector has the armor I gave him to wear? As for me, I do not care to live unless I can take revenge on Hector.”
Then Thetis said: “No, my son, do not talk like that. When Hector dies, your own doom is near.”

And Achilles said in great anger: “I wish I could die this very hour, since I could not help my friend and am only a burden on the earth, I, who am better in battle than all the other Greeks. Cursed be the anger that sets men fighting one another, just as it set me fighting with King Agamemnon! But let the past be past. As for my fate, let it come when it will, as long as I first take revenge on Hector. So do not try to hold me back from the battle.”
Then Thetis said: “So be it. But you cannot go without your armor, and Hector has it. Tomorrow I will go to Hephæstus and ask him to make you new armor.”

While they talked, the Trojans kept pressing the Greeks harder. The two heroes, Ajax the Greater and Ajax the Less, could no longer stop Hector from getting hold of the body of Patroclus, and he would surely have seized it. But Zeus sent Iris to Achilles with this message:—
“Get up, son of Peleus, or the dogs of Troy will have Patroclus!”
Achilles answered, “How can I go? I have no armor, and I don’t know whose I could wear.”
Iris replied, “Just go to the trench and show yourself. The Trojans will tremble and stop fighting, and the Greeks will get a moment to catch their breath.”

So he went to the trench. He did not join the fighting, because he was obeying his mother’s orders, but he shouted aloud, and his voice rang like a trumpet. When the Trojans heard it, they were struck with fear. The horses shied back with the chariots, and the drivers stared in amazement at the blazing fire above his head, which Athene had lit. Three times the great Achilles shouted across the trench, and three times the Trojans fell back. In that hour twelve famous chiefs died, wounded by their own spears or trampled by their own horses, so great was the terror among the Trojans.
The Greeks gladly pulled Patroclus out of the crush of battle. They laid him on a bier and carried him to the tent, with Achilles walking beside him, weeping bitterly.

chapters.title: The Making of the Arms
paragraphs: Achilles stood among his Myrmidons and said:—

“The promise I made to Menœtius was empty. I told him I would bring his son home with his share of the spoils of Troy. Instead Patroclus lies dead, and I will never go back to the house of my father Peleus, for I too must die in this land. But I will not bury you, Patroclus, until I bring here the head and the armor of Hector, and twelve Trojans to be killed at your funeral fire.”
Men-œ’-ti-us.

Then they washed the body of Patroclus and rubbed it with oil. They filled his wounds with ointment nine years old, laid him on a bed, covered him from head to foot with a linen cloth, and spread a white robe over it. All night the Myrmidons mourned for the dead Patroclus.

Meanwhile Thetis went to the house of Hephæstus. She found him busy at his work, making twenty three-legged cauldrons to stand around the house of the gods. He had put golden wheels beneath them, so that they could roll by themselves into the halls of the gods and return again on their own. Grace, the wife of Hephæstus, saw Thetis, took her by the hands, led her in, and sat her on a silver-studded chair with a footstool under her feet. Then she called to her husband:—
“Come quickly. Thetis needs something from you.”

He said, “Truly, she saved me in my time of trouble. My mother threw me out because I was lame, but Thetis and her sister took me in under the sea. I lived with them for nine years and hammered out many a trinket in a hollow cave. I would give my life for Thetis.”

Then he put away his tools, washed himself, took a staff in his hand, and came into the house. He sat down on a chair and said, “Tell me everything that is on your mind. I will do what you wish, if it can be done.”
Thetis told him about her son Achilles, about the wrong that had been done to him and his anger, and about how Patroclus was dead and the armor Achilles had once owned was lost.
“Please make him a shield and a helmet,” she said, “and greaves and a corselet.”
greaves, armor for the legs.
Hephæstus answered, “Take heart. I wish I could keep death away from him as easily as I can make him armor that will make people marvel when they look at it.”

Then he went to his forge and turned the bellows toward the fire and told them to get to work. He threw bronze, tin, gold, and silver into the fire to melt, set up the anvil, and took the hammer in one hand and the tongs in the other.

First he made a great, strong shield and fastened a silver strap to it. On it he worked the earth, the sky, the sea, the sun, the moon, and all the stars. He also made two cities. One was at peace, and the other was at war. In the first, people were leading a bride to her new home with music and dancing, while the women stood in their doorways to watch. Around the other city sat an army laying siege to it, and the men of the city stood on the wall to defend it. They had also set an ambush by a river where the herds usually came to drink. When the herds came down, the men jumped up, drove off the animals, and killed the herdsmen. But the besieging army heard the outcry, rode up quickly on horses, and fought on the riverbank. He also made a field where many men were plowing, and another where reapers were cutting the grain while boys gathered it in their arms to tie into sheaves, and the landowner stood by, glad at heart, watching them. He made a vineyard, too, with a path through it, and young men and girls carrying baskets of grapes, and in the middle a boy playing a golden harp and singing a pleasant song. He made a herd of oxen going from the stables to the pastures, with herdsmen and dogs, and at the front two lions had seized a mighty bull and were devouring it, while the dogs stood far off and barked. He made a sheepfold, and a wonderful dance of young men and girls, who wore golden crowns, while the men had golden daggers hanging from silver belts. And all around the edge of the shield he worked the great river of Ocean.

Besides the shield, he made a corselet brighter than fire, a great helmet with a golden ridge for its crest, and greaves of tin. When he had finished all the armor, he set it before the mother of Achilles. She swooped down from Olympus like a hawk, carrying it to her son. When she reached the ships, she found him lying on the ground with his arms around the body of Patroclus, weeping aloud, while his men stood around him mourning.
