The goddess stood in the midst of them, took her son by the hand, and said, “Come, let us leave the dead man. He was killed because the gods willed it. Now take this armor from Hephæstus. It is more beautiful than anything a man has ever worn on his shoulders.”

With that she threw the armor down in front of Achilles. It clanged loudly as it fell, and the Myrmidons were afraid to look at it. But Achilles picked up the splendid armor and was glad. He said, “Mother, the gods have given me armor fit to be made in heaven, and I swear I will put it on for the fight. But I am afraid that decay will spoil the body of Patroclus, now that the life has gone out of it.”

Thetis answered, “Don’t let that trouble you. I will keep decay from his flesh, even if he lies here until the year comes round again. Go now, call the people to an assembly, give up your anger against King Agamemnon, and arm yourself for battle.”
As she spoke, she filled his soul with trust and courage. Into the dead man’s nostrils she poured ambrosia and red nectar, so that his flesh would stay sweet.

chapters.title: The Ending of the Strife
paragraphs: Achilles walked along the seashore, calling out to the warriors. They came at his call, and Diomed and Ulysses came to the assembly too, leaning on their spears because their wounds were still fresh, and so did King Agamemnon.

Achilles stood up and said, “Son of Atreus, it was a mistake for us to quarrel over a woman! I wish Artemis had killed her with an arrow the day I took her captive! Many a Greek who now lies biting the dust would still be alive, and the Trojans would not have gained so much from our anger. But come, let the past be past. Here I put an end to my anger. Now hurry, and send the Greeks into battle. Let us see whether the Trojans will camp beside the ships.”

Then Agamemnon spoke from where he sat. “Listen, Greeks. You have often blamed me for this quarrel. But it was not my fault. It was Zeus and Fate and the Fury who walks in darkness. To you, Achilles, I will make full amends. I offer you the gifts that Ulysses promised you yesterday. Wait a little while my people bring them from my ships.”
Achilles answered him, “Give the gifts, King, if you wish, or keep them for yourself. But let us go to the battle without delay.”

Then the wise Ulysses spoke. “Achilles, don’t urge the Greeks to go into battle on empty stomachs, because the fight will not be short. A man who has not eaten cannot keep fighting until sunset. His limbs grow heavy without his noticing, and hunger and thirst wear him down. So tell the people to scatter and prepare their meal. Meanwhile, let King Agamemnon send for the gifts and hand them over to you in front of the whole assembly. Afterward, let him provide a feast.”
The King said, “You speak well, Ulysses. Go and fetch the gifts yourself, and let the herald bring us a boar, so that we can sacrifice to Zeus and to the Sun.”

But Achilles said, “The men Hector killed lie dead, and you tell me to think about food. Let the Greeks go into battle fasting, and let them have a great supper when the sun goes down. As for me, no food or drink will pass my lips.”

Ulysses replied, “You are the stronger, son of Peleus, but I may be the wiser, because I am older than you and have more experience. Don’t ask the Greeks to fast because of the dead. Men fall every day. Instead, let us bury whoever dies, mourn him for a day, and harden our hearts to forget. Then let those of us who are left eat and drink, so that we can fight with better courage.”
Then Ulysses went to the King’s tent, and they brought out the gifts from there: the treasure, twelve horses, seven women skilled at needlework, and the fair Briseis as the eighth.

The Myrmidons took these to the tent of Achilles. When Briseis saw Patroclus, she beat her breast and struck her lovely face and neck and wailed aloud, because, she said, he had been gentle and good. All the women wailed with her, each thinking of her own sorrows.

Then the chiefs urged Achilles to feast with them, but he would not listen, because he refused to eat or drink until he had taken revenge for the dead. He said, “Patroclus, you often set out the feast for us when we were hurrying to the war. Now you lie dead, and in my grief for you I cannot eat or drink. No greater sorrow could have come to me. I often thought that I alone would die here, and that you would go home and show my son everything that was mine, my goods and servants and palace.”
While he wept, the elders wept along with him, and each of them remembered what he had left behind at home.
Then Zeus said to Athene, “Don’t you care about Achilles, who is so dear to you? Look, the other Greeks have gone to their meal, but he sits there fasting.”
Athene leapt down from heaven and poured nectar and ambrosia into the chest of Achilles, so that his knees would not give way from hunger.

Meanwhile the Greeks poured out to battle, and in the middle of them Achilles put on his armor. He strapped the splendid greaves to his legs and fitted the corselet on his chest. He hung the sword from his shoulders, and picked up the great shield that Hephæstus had made, which blazed like the sky. He put the helmet on his head, and the plumes waved all around it. Then he tried out the armor, and it fit him well and lifted him up like wings. Last, he drew his father’s spear from its case, which no one but Achilles himself could wield. Then he spoke to his horses: “Be careful, Bayard and Piebald. Bring your driver back safely today, and don’t leave him dead on the field the way you left Patroclus.”

Then Hera gave the horse Bayard a voice, and he spoke: “We will certainly save you, great Achilles. Even so, your death is near. We are not the cause of it, but the gods and mighty Fate. It was not our fault that Patroclus died. Apollo killed him and gave the glory to Hector. You too will die at the hands of a god and a mortal man.”
Achilles said, “Why tell me about my doom? I know it very well. But I will not stop until I have made the Trojans sick of battle.”

chapters.title: The Battle at the River
paragraphs: So Achilles went into battle again, eager above all else to meet Hector and kill him.
But Apollo stood beside Æneas and said to him, “Æneas, what has become of your boasts that you would face Achilles?”

Æneas answered, “No, I have stood against him before, on the day he took the town of Lyrnessus. But I ran from him, and only my quick feet saved me from his spear. A god is surely always with him, making his spear fly true.”
Lyr-nes’-sus.

Apollo answered him again: “You too are the son of a goddess, and your mother is greater than his, for she is only a daughter of the Sea. Charge straight at him with your spear, and don’t let his threats frighten you.”

Then Æneas threw his spear. It struck the shield of Achilles with such a terrible sound that the hero was afraid it would go right through, not knowing that gifts of the gods are not easy for a mortal to overcome. The spear did pierce two layers of bronze, but the gold stopped it, and there were still two layers of tin behind. Then Achilles threw his spear. It went through the shield of Æneas, and although it did not wound him, he was badly shaken, for it came so close. Then Achilles drew his sword and rushed at Æneas, and Æneas snatched up a great stone to throw at him. But the gods did not will that Æneas should die, since he and his descendants were to rule the Trojans in the ages to come. So Poseidon lifted him up and carried him over the ranks of men to the left side of the battle, but first he pulled the spear out of the shield and laid it at the feet of Achilles. The hero was amazed to see it, and cried, “This is a great wonder I see with my own eyes. My spear lies before me, but the man I tried to kill is nowhere to be seen. Truly Æneas was telling the truth when he said the immortal gods loved him.”

Then he plunged into the fighting, killing as he went. Hector would have faced him, but Apollo stood beside him and warned: “Do not fight Achilles, or he will kill you.” So Hector drew back among the Trojan ranks. Achilles killed many men, and among them Polydorus, a son of Priam. Because Polydorus was the youngest and very dear to him, his father had not allowed him to go into battle. But he went anyway, foolishly, and since he was a very fast runner, he trusted his speed and darted along the front lines of the fighters. As he ran, Achilles struck him down and gave him a mortal wound. When Hector saw this, he could no longer bear to stand aside. He rushed at Achilles, and Achilles was glad to see him come. “Here is the man who killed my friend,” he said, and he shouted to Hector, “Come here and taste death.”
Pol-y-do’-rus.
Hector answered: “Son of Peleus, don’t try to frighten me with words. I may be weaker than you, but victory rests in the hands of the gods, and I carry a spear too.”

Then he hurled his spear, but Athene turned it aside with a puff of her breath and sent it back to land at his feet. When Achilles sprang at Hector with a shout, Apollo swept him away. Three times Achilles charged at him, and three times he struck only mist. The fourth time he screamed in a terrible voice, “You dog! You escaped death because Apollo helped you, but I will meet you again and finish you.”

Then Achilles turned on the rest and killed great numbers of them, so that they ran, some across the plain and some toward the river, the swirling Xanthus. They jumped into the water the way locusts leap into a river when a fire that men have lit drives them out of the fields. The whole river filled with horses and men. Then Achilles jumped into the stream, leaving his spear on the bank, leaning against the tamarisk trees. He had only his sword, and with it he killed many more; they were like fish fleeing from a huge dolphin in the sea. When Achilles grew tired of killing, he took twelve men alive, to be slaughtered on the tomb of Patroclus.
Then Asteropæus came to meet him, a grandson of the river-god Axius. Achilles was amazed to see him, and he asked, “Who are you, that you dare to stand against me?”
As-ter-o-pæ’-us. Ax’-i-us.
He answered, “I am the grandson of the river-god Axius, the loveliest of all the streams on earth.”

As he spoke, he threw two spears at once, one from each hand, for he could use both hands equally well. One spear hit the shield but did not go through, because the gold stopped it; the other grazed Achilles’ right hand, and the blood spurted out. Then Achilles threw his own spear, but he missed, and the great spear stuck fast in the bank. Three times Asteropæus tried to pull it out, and three times he failed. The fourth time he tried to break it. But while he was struggling, Achilles struck him and he died. Still, he had won some glory, for he had wounded the great Achilles.

chapters.title: The Battle of the Gods
paragraphs: When the River saw that Asteropæus was dead, he took the shape of a man and spoke to Achilles: “Truly, Achilles, you surpass all other men in strength and in bloody deeds, because the gods themselves protect you. Perhaps Zeus has given you the power to kill every son of Troy. But leave me now and do as you please out on the plain, because my stream is clogged with corpses, and I cannot flow out to the sea. So stop troubling me.”

Achilles answered him: “It will be as you wish, Scamander. But I will not stop killing the Trojans until I have driven them into their city and tested myself against Hector, to see whether I will defeat him or he will defeat me.”

With these words he rushed on, chasing the Trojans. Then the River called to Apollo: “You with the Silver Bow, you are doing very little of what your father wants. He ordered you to stand by the men of Troy and help them until darkness covered the land.” And the River surged forward in a great wave, stirring all his streams together. He threw the dead bodies onto the shore, roaring like a bull, and he hid the living in the depths of his whirlpools. The flood rose all around Achilles and beat down on his shield, so that he could not keep his footing. Achilles grabbed hold of a tall, beautiful lime tree that grew on the bank, but the tree was torn out with all its roots, and it ripped away the bank and fell across the River. Because it had so many branches, it dammed up the flow. Then Achilles jumped out of the water and ran across the plain in great fear. But the River did not stop chasing him, since he meant to keep Achilles from the killing and save the sons of Troy. Achilles leaped as far as a man can throw a spear. Still the River followed behind him with a mighty roar.

When Achilles tried to make a stand against the River, wanting to find out whether all the gods were truly against him, the great wave crashed onto his shoulders. When he jumped into the air, the wave buckled his knees and washed the ground out from under his feet. Then Achilles looked up at the sky and groaned: “Zeus, will none of the gods pity me and save me from the River? I don’t care what else happens to me. My mother lied to me when she said I would die beneath the walls of Troy from the arrows of Apollo. It would have been better if Hector had killed me, for he is the bravest man in Troy. But now I will die a miserable death in the River, like a young shepherd boy swept away by a torrent in a storm.”

So he spoke, but Poseidon and Athene stood beside him, having taken the shape of men. They took him by the hand and gave him strength with comforting words, and Poseidon said: “Son of Peleus, do not tremble or be afraid. It is not your fate to be beaten by the River. He will soon stop troubling you. Now listen to what we say. Do not hold back from the fighting until you have driven all the sons of Troy who escape you inside the walls of the city. And when you have killed Hector, go back to the ships; this day will be the day of your glory.”

Then the two left him. By now the whole plain was flooded, and many fine suits of armor and many dead bodies floated on the water. But Achilles pushed on straight against the current, and the River could not hold him back, because Athene had filled his heart with great strength. Yet Scamander did not give up his anger. He raised his waves higher and shouted to Simois: “Dear brother, let us two stop this man’s fury, or he will surely destroy the city of Priam. Come, fill all your streams, rouse your torrents against him, and send up a mighty wave full of tree trunks and stones, so that we can stop this wild man from fighting. Neither his strength, nor his good looks, nor his handsome form will help him, because they will be buried under thick mud. I will heap sand over him, more than anyone could count. The Greeks will never be able to gather up his bones, because I will hide them under such a mound.”
Si’-mo-is.

Then the River rushed at Achilles again, swelling high with foam and blood and the bodies of dead men. The wave rose very dark and seemed about to overwhelm him, so that Hera was terribly afraid the River would sweep him away. She called to her son Hephæstus: “Get up, Haltfoot, my son! Come and help us, and bring plenty of fire. I will call the west wind and the south wind up from the sea, with a storm that will consume the sons of Troy, men and weapons together. And you, burn the trees along the banks of the Xanthus, and the River himself too. Don’t let him turn you from your purpose with rage or with tricks. Keep burning until I tell you to stop.”

Then Hephæstus lit a great fire. First it burned the dead bodies lying on the plain, and it dried out the whole plain, the way the north wind in autumn dries a field, to the joy of the farmer who works it. After that it turned on the River. It burned the lime tree, the willows, and the tamarisks, and the plants that grew in the streams. The eels and the fish were in terrible distress, twisting this way and that in the water, tormented by the breath of Hephæstus. So the River’s power was broken, and he cried out: “Hephæstus, none of the gods can match you. Stop burning me now. Achilles can drive the men of Troy out of the city if he wants. What do I have to do with the strife and sorrow of men?”
Queen Hera heard him and called to Hephæstus: “That is enough, my son. It is not right for you to do such harm to a god for the sake of a mortal man.”
So Hephæstus put out his fire, and the River flowed in his bed again as before.

But among the other gods a terrible quarrel broke out, and they split into two sides, one against the other. They came together with a mighty crash, and the wide earth echoed and the heavens rang like a trumpet. Zeus heard it as he sat on Olympus, and he was glad in his heart to see the gods join in battle.

Ares, who pierces shields, was the first to charge at Athene. He held his spear and shouted: “Why do you make the gods fight each other, you who are as bold as a fly and as shameless as a dog? Don’t you remember how you set Diomed, the son of Tydeus, on me to wound me, and how you took his spear in your own hand, where everyone could see, and drove it through my thigh? Now I will pay you back for everything you have done.”

And he struck her shield, the mighty shield that not even the thunder of Zeus can break. But Athene picked up a huge stone that lay on the plain. It was black and rough and enormous, and men of long ago had set it there to mark the boundary of a field. With this she struck Ares on the neck, and his knees gave way beneath him. He lay stretched on the ground, covering more than a hundred feet, and Athene laughed when she saw him. She cried: “Fool! Haven’t you learned yet how much stronger I am than you, that you dare to match your strength against mine? Lie there and take your mother’s curses, because she is furious that you have betrayed the Greeks and are helping the men of Troy.”

But Aphrodite took Ares by the hand and tried to lead him away. He groaned deeply and could hardly pull himself together. When Hera saw this, she called to Athene: “Look how Aphrodite is leading Ares out of the battle! Go after her and stop her.”

So Athene went after her and struck her on the chest with her heavy hand, and Aphrodite’s knees gave way. So these two lay on the ground, and Athene shouted over them: “I wish everyone who helps the sons of Troy were as brave and strong as these two. We would have ended the war long ago and destroyed the lovely city of Troy.”

chapters.title: The Slaying of Hector
paragraphs: While all this was going on, Achilles kept chasing and killing the men of Troy, and Priam stood on a tower of the wall and watched his people. He was deeply troubled, and he hurried down to the gates and told the guards, “Keep the gates open so the people can come in, because they are running from Achilles.” So the guards held the gates open, and the people hurried in, exhausted from the struggle and from thirst, and covered with dust, and Achilles followed close behind them. At that hour the Greeks would have taken the city of Troy, if Apollo had not saved it. He put courage into the heart of Agenor and stood beside him, so that he would not be killed. And Agenor thought to himself:
A-ge’-nor.

“Should I run away with all the others? No, because Achilles will catch me and kill me, and I will die like a coward. Or should I run across the plain to Mount Ida and hide in the thickets, then come back to the city at nightfall? But if he sees me, he will catch me and strike me down, because he is so fast and strong. What if I stand and face him in front of the gates? He too is a mortal man, and a spear can pierce his flesh.”

So he stood and waited for Achilles to come near. When Achilles came, Agenor threw his spear and hit him in the leg below the knee, but the shin guard turned the spear aside, it was so strong. When Achilles was about to kill him, suddenly Apollo lifted Agenor up and set him down inside the city. And to give the men of Troy time to get in, Apollo took on Agenor’s shape. The false Agenor ran, and Achilles chased him. Meanwhile the men of Troy poured into the city, and in such haste and fear were they running that they did not stop to ask who was safe and who was dead. Only Hector stayed outside the walls, standing in front of the great Scæan gates. All this time Achilles was chasing the false Agenor furiously, until at last Apollo turned around and spoke to him:

“Why are you chasing me, swift-footed Achilles? Haven’t you figured out yet that I am a god, and that all your rage is for nothing? Now all the sons of Troy are safe inside their city, and you are here, far out of the way, trying to kill me, who cannot die.”

Achilles answered him in great anger: “You have wronged me by drawing me away from the wall, great archer, you who love mischief more than any other god. If not for that, many more Trojans would have bitten the dust. You have robbed me of great glory and saved the men you favor. If only I had the power to take revenge on you! You would pay dearly for your trick!”

Then he turned and rushed toward the city, as fast as a racehorse pulling a chariot across the plain. Old Priam saw him from the walls, his armor glittering as bright as the brightest of the stars, the one men call Orion’s Dog, which shines at harvest time. The old man groaned aloud when he saw him, and he stretched out his hands and called to his son Hector, who stood before the gates, eager to fight this terrible warrior:
O-ri’-on.

“Don’t wait for this man, dear son, don’t wait for him, or you will die by his hand, because he is truly stronger than you. Come inside the walls, dear child; come and save the sons and daughters of Troy; come out of pity for me, your father, for whom an evil fate waits in my old age: to see my sons killed by the sword, my daughters carried off as captives, and little babies dashed to the ground.”

His mother begged him too, but it was no use. He was still determined to wait for Achilles to come. It was like a great snake in the mountains, waiting at its hole for a man to approach: its eyes glare fiercely and it coils its tail around the hole. That is how Hector waited for Achilles.

Achilles came closer, swinging his great spear up over his right shoulder, and the blaze of his armor was like fire, or like the rising sun. Hector shook with fear at the sight of him and did not dare to wait for him. He bolted from the gates, with Achilles close behind, the way a hawk, swiftest of all birds, swoops after a dove in the mountains. They raced past the watchtower and the wind-swept fig tree, along the wagon road that circled the walls, until they reached the clear, flowing fountain where the two springs of the swirling Scamander well up.

They ran on past the springs, one running away and the other chasing him. The one who fled was brave, but the one who chased was braver. This was no race for a sheep to sacrifice or a shield of oxhide; the prize was the life of Hector, the tamer of horses. Three times they circled the city, and all the gods watched.

Then Zeus spoke. “What I am seeing is a pitiful thing. My heart aches for Hector—Hector, who has always honored me with sacrifices—and now the mighty Achilles is hunting him around the city of Priam. Come, gods, let us decide together. Shall we save him from death, or let him fall to Achilles?”
Athene answered, “What are you saying, great father?—to rescue a man whom fate has marked out to die? Do it if you wish, but the rest of us gods will not approve.”
Zeus replied, “I am reluctant, but I want to please you. Have it your way.”

Athene hurried down from the peak of Olympus. Meanwhile Hector kept running and Achilles kept chasing, like a dog after a fawn in the hills. Again and again Hector headed for the gates, or for the shelter of the towers, hoping the men standing there could defend him with their spears; and again and again Achilles cut in ahead of him and forced him back toward the plain. So they ran, one trying to reach the city and the other driving him out to the plain.

Achilles had signaled to the Greeks that no one should throw a spear at Hector, in case someone else took the glory from him. When the two came to the springs of Scamander for the fourth time, Zeus held out his great scales of fate. In one pan he put the fate of Achilles and in the other the fate of Hector. And look! Hector’s pan sank down toward the land of the dead, and Apollo abandoned him.

Athene swooped down from the sky to Achilles’ side and said, “Great Achilles, today we win glory, for we will kill Hector, mighty warrior though he is. He is fated to die, and not even Apollo himself can save him. Stand still now and catch your breath, and I will put courage into this man to face you in battle.”
So Achilles stopped and leaned on his spear. Athene took the shape of Deiphobus, went up to Hector, and said:
De-iph’-o-bus.
“Achilles is pressing you hard, my brother, chasing you like this around the city of Priam. Come, let us make a stand and face him together.”
Hector answered, “Deiphobus, you were always my favorite of all my brothers, but now I love you even more. While all the others stayed inside, you alone have dared to come out and stand beside me.”

The false Deiphobus said, “My father and mother and all my friends begged me to stay. But my heart was heavy for you, and I could not. Come, let us stand and fight this man, and find out whether he will carry off our spoils to his ships, or whether we will kill him here.”

The two warriors came face to face, and Hector of the waving plume spoke first. “Three times, great Achilles, you chased me around the walls of Troy, and I did not dare to stand against you. Now I am no longer afraid of you. But let us make one agreement. If Zeus gives me the victory, I will not disgrace your body. I will take your weapons and armor and give your body back to the Greeks. Promise that you will do the same for me.”

Achilles glared at him and said, “Hector, do not talk to me about agreements. Men and lions do not swear oaths with each other, and wolves and sheep never come to terms. There will be no agreement between you and me. One of us will fall. Now is the time to prove you are a warrior, for Athene will surely kill you with my spear, and you will pay for all my comrades whom you have slain.”

Then he hurled his mighty spear. Hector saw it coming and ducked low to the ground, so that the spear flew over his head and stuck in the earth. But Athene pulled it out and handed it back to Achilles, without Hector noticing.
Hector called to Achilles, “You missed, great Achilles. Now watch out for my spear. I wish it would sink deep into your flesh! The war would be easier for the men of Troy if you were out of the way.”

With those words he threw his long spear, and his aim was true: it hit the very center of Achilles’ shield. But it did not break through. It bounced far away, for that shield was no mortal work. Hector stood stunned, because he had no second spear. He called to Deiphobus to bring him another, and look! Deiphobus was gone. Then Hector knew his end had come, and he said to himself, “So the gods have called me to my doom. I thought Deiphobus was beside me, but he is inside the walls, and the help he promised was a trick that Athene played on me. Zeus and Apollo are no longer with me. But if I must die, let me at least die doing something that people in later times will hear about.”

With that he drew the great sword that hung at his side and, like an eagle diving through the clouds to snatch a lamb, he flew at the mighty Achilles. But he never landed a blow. Achilles charged to meet him, with his shield in front of his chest and his helmet tipped forward as he ran, the long plumes streaming behind, and his spear point gleamed like the evening star, the loveliest star in the sky. For a moment he considered where to strike, since the armor Hector had taken from Patroclus protected him well. But there was one spot, where the neck meets the shoulder by the collarbone, and nowhere is a sword or spear thrust more deadly. Achilles drove the spear in there, the point came out through the back of the neck, and Hector fell in the dust.

Achilles shouted, “Hector, when you stripped Patroclus of his armor, you thought you would be safe from revenge. And look! You have fallen before me. Now the dogs and vultures will devour you, while all the Greeks will give him a proper burial.”

Hector, growing faint, said to him, “No, great Achilles, I beg you by your life, by your knees, and by your dear parents, do not let the Greeks’ dogs devour me. Take instead the ransom of gold and bronze that my father and mother will pay you, and let the sons and daughters of Troy give me a funeral.”

Achilles glared at him and cried, “Dog, do not try to plead with me! I could carve up your flesh and eat it raw, after the grief you have caused me. The dogs will certainly devour you, and no one will stop them. Not if they offered ten times the ransom, not even if Priam offered your weight in gold, would I sell you back.”

Then Hector, who was now close to death, said to him, “I know you well, and I know what you are: the heart in your chest is nothing but iron. Just be careful that the gods do not take revenge on you on the day when Paris and Apollo kill you, for all your courage, at the Scæan gates.”
With these words he died. Achilles answered, “Die, hound! As for my own fate, I will meet it whenever Zeus and the other gods decide.”

Then he pulled his spear out of the body and stripped off the armor. All the Greeks gathered around the dead man, marveling at how tall and handsome he was, and every one of them wounded the corpse. One would say to another, “This Hector is certainly less frightening now than when he was setting our ships on fire.”

Then Achilles thought of something ruthless. He pierced Hector’s ankle bones and tied the body to his chariot with oxhide straps, leaving the head to drag behind, that head which had been so handsome and was now so ruined in the dust. In this way he dragged Hector to the ships. Priam saw it from the walls, and his sons could barely hold him back from going out to beg for the body of his dear son from the man who had killed him. Hecuba, Hector’s mother, also wept aloud, but Andromache did not yet know what had happened. She was sitting in her house, weaving a great purple cloak embroidered with flowers. She had told her maids to prepare a bath for Hector for when he returned from the battle, not knowing that he would never need it again. But the sound of wailing from the town reached her. She jumped up in great fear, dropped the shuttle from her hand, and called to her maids:

“Come with me, maids, so that I can find out what has happened. I heard Queen Hecuba’s voice, and I am afraid that something terrible has come upon the children of Priam. Perhaps Achilles has cut Hector off from the city and is chasing him out onto the plain, because Hector will never stay back with the army. He always fights in the front, he is so bold.”

She rushed through the city as if she were mad. When she reached the wall, she stopped and looked out. And there, Achilles’ horses were dragging Hector to the ships! Darkness covered her eyes, and she fell back in a faint.

chapters.title: The Burning of Patroclus
paragraphs: While the Trojans mourned for Hector in the city, the Greeks went back to their camp. The others scattered, each to his own ship, but Achilles spoke to the Myrmidons. “Do not unhitch your horses,” he said. “Let us honor Patroclus by driving our chariots around his body, mourning as we go.”

The Myrmidons did as he asked. Three times they drove their chariots around the dead man, and they mourned, with Achilles leading them. He also laid Hector’s body in the dust beside the dead man. After that he held a funeral feast for his people. The chiefs had to bring him, very much against his will, to King Agamemnon, who had given a great feast for the Greek leaders. When the heralds heated water in a cauldron and wanted him to wash off the blood, he refused. “No,” he said. “Water will not come near me until I have laid Patroclus on the fire and heaped a mound over him. Now let us eat our meal, even though we are grieving. Tomorrow we will give the dead man his full honors.”
They ate and drank their fill. Then the rest lay down to sleep in their own tents, while Achilles stayed out in an open place on the seashore, among his Myrmidons, groaning deeply.

The next day they built a great pile of wood and laid the dead man on top of it. Patroclus had owned nine dogs, and Achilles killed two of them on the pile. He killed four horses too, and also the twelve young Trojans he had captured at the river. Then he set the pile on fire and said, “Hear me, Patroclus: twelve sons of Troy are burning with you in the fire. But Hector I will give to the dogs.”

When the burning was almost over, Achilles said, “Put out the remaining fire with wine, and gather the bones of Patroclus from where they lie apart in the middle of the pile. Put them in a golden urn, to keep until the day I die. Build a tomb over them that is not too large. When I am dead too, those of you who are left can make it higher, as is right.”

When all this was done, Achilles wanted to show the dead man every honor, so he announced games in which the chiefs would compete against one another. He called the people together and brought out of his ships many things to serve as prizes: cauldrons, bronze kettles, horses and mules, fair women-slaves, and iron.

First he held a chariot race. For the first prize he set out a woman-slave skilled in all the work of the loom, together with a bronze kettle. The second prize was a six-year-old mare; the third, a fine new bronze kettle; the fourth, two talents of gold; and the fifth, a double cup. Then he stood up in the middle of the crowd and spoke. “Men of Greece, look at these prizes that I have set out for a chariot race. If we were honoring anyone other than Patroclus, I would take the first prize to my own tent, because there are no horses in the camp like mine. They are not even of mortal breed; Poseidon gave them to my father, Peleus. But I will stay out of this race, and so will my horses, because the man who drove them is dead, and they loved him. They stand grieving, with their manes drooping to the ground.” Then five chiefs stepped forward. First was Eumelus, then Diomed, with the horses of Troy that he had taken from Æneas. Third was Menelaus, driving his horse Whitefoot and a mare called Flash-of-Fire. Fourth came Antilochus, son of Nestor, and after him Meriones.
Eu-me’-lus.

Next they drew lots for their starting places. The first lot fell to Antilochus, then came Eumelus, Menelaus, Meriones, and Diomed, in that order. Achilles marked out the course and appointed old Phœnix as judge. Then the race began. The drivers raised their whips and lashed their horses, shouting as they went. Dust billowed up around the horses’ chests, their manes streamed in the wind, and the chariots seemed to skim the ground one moment and leap into the air the next. But as the drivers neared the turning-point at the far end of the course, it became clear which horses were the better ones. The horses of Eumelus were in front, and right behind them came those of King Diomed, so close that they seemed ready to trample the chariot ahead, and the back and broad shoulders of Eumelus were warm with their breath. Diomed would have passed him then, or at least drawn level, but Apollo begrudged him the victory, since the god did not love him, and knocked the whip from his hand. Diomed was furious, and his eyes filled with tears to see his horses running out of control. But Athene saw what had happened and pitied him. She gave him back his whip and put new strength into his horses. Then she went to Eumelus and broke the yoke of his chariot, so that the pole dug into the ground and he was thrown out, with badly bruised elbows, mouth, and nostrils, and a gash on his forehead above the eyebrows. So Diomed took the lead, with Menelaus next. Then Antilochus shouted to his horses: “Run as fast as you can! I’m not telling you to race the horses of King Diomed, because Athene gives them speed and strength. But you can catch the horses of Menelaus. It would be a disgrace if Flame-of-Fire, a mare, left you behind.”

The horses were afraid of the prince’s anger and sprang forward. Now Antilochus had noticed a narrow spot in the road, where winter floods had broken it away. As Menelaus drove his chariot past it, Antilochus swung a little off the track and tried to get by at the same moment. There was not room for two chariots, and Menelaus grew alarmed and shouted: “Why are you driving so recklessly, Antilochus? Hold back a moment, and you can pass me where the road is wider. Here you will wreck your chariot and mine.” But Antilochus drove on even harder, pretending not to hear. For about the distance of a quoit’s throw the two chariots ran side by side, and then Menelaus drew back, afraid they would crash together. But he called out to Antilochus: “Was there ever a man so spiteful as you? Still, you will not win this prize unless you are willing to swear falsely that you played fair!” Then he called to his horses: “Go on! Don’t stop. You will catch them, because their horses will tire before you do.”
Meanwhile the Greeks sat waiting for the chariots to come back.

Diomed came in first and leaped down from his chariot. Antilochus was next, having beaten Menelaus by trickery rather than speed. Still, Menelaus was not far behind, only as far as a chariot is from the horse that pulls it, so fast was the mare Flame-of-Fire, though at the start he had been a full quoit’s throw back. But Meriones lost by a spear’s flight, because his horses were the slowest and he was a less skilled driver. Last of all came Eumelus, pulling his chariot himself and driving his horses ahead of him. Achilles felt sorry for him and said: “The most skilled driver comes in last. Surely he should get the second prize.”

The Greeks agreed, but Antilochus cried out: “Will you take this prize from me because his chariot was broken? If he had prayed to the gods, it would not have happened. If you pity him, give him something of your own. As for this prize, no one takes it from me except by force of arms.”
Achilles laughed and said: “Well said, Antilochus. I will give him something of my own, a breastplate that Asteropæus wore.”

Then Menelaus stood up, deeply angry, and said: “What have you done, Antilochus? You have shamed me and my horses by putting your own ahead of them, though they are in truth much worse. So judge between us, chiefs of the Greeks. And you, Antilochus, stand in front of your chariot and horses as custom requires, holding your whip in one hand and laying the other on your horses, and swear by Poseidon that you did not block my chariot by fraud.”

Antilochus answered him: “Forgive me, Menelaus. I am younger than you, and you know how young men go wrong, since their judgment is hasty and their wits are small. As for the mare, I give her to you, and anything else you want, rather than quarrel with you or sin against the gods.”

Menelaus’s heart was glad, as the grain is glad when dew falls on it. He said: “Well spoken, son of Nestor. And now—because your father and your brother have suffered much for my sake—I give you this mare.”

Menelaus himself took the bronze kettle, and Meriones had the fourth prize. The double cup Achilles gave to old Nestor, saying: “Take this as a keepsake of the burial of Patroclus, whom you will not see again. I know that old age keeps you from wrestling or boxing with the others.”

After this Achilles set out two prizes for boxers: a mule for the winner, and a cup with two mouths for the loser. Epeius stood up and said: “Who wants this cup? No one but me will take the mule. I am weak in battle—but what man can do everything?—yet whoever stands against me today, I swear I will tear his flesh and break his bones, so his friends had better be close by to carry him away.”
E-pei’-us.

Euryalus rose to face him. King Diomed stood beside him, badly wanting him to win, and brought him his belt to put on and gave him the heavy gloves of bull’s hide. Then the two men stood together in the middle of the ring. They traded many blows, so loud that they were dreadful to hear, and the sweat poured off them. But after a while Epeius lunged and struck Euryalus on the jaw, right through his guard, and Euryalus could not stand up to it. As a fish is flung onto the shore by the north wind, so he was thrown to the ground. Epeius lifted him up, and his friends led him away, badly hurt and dazed.
Eu-ry’-a-lus.

Next Achilles called for a wrestling match. The winner would receive a great bronze kettle worth twelve oxen, and the loser a woman slave skilled at the loom, worth four oxen. Ajax the Greater and Ulysses stood up, gripped each other with their hands, and struggled for the upper hand. After a while, when neither could win and the crowd was tired of watching, Ajax said: “Come, Ulysses. Either you lift me off the ground, or I lift you. Then we can settle this.” Ajax grabbed Ulysses to lift him, and he would have done it, but Ulysses used a trick, as he always did. He hooked his leg behind Ajax’s knee and struck the tendon, so that Ajax fell, and Ulysses fell on top of him. Then Ulysses tried to lift Ajax; he raised him a little way but could not get him up, and his own knee gave way, and they both fell to the ground. When they were about to go at it a third time, Achilles stopped them, saying: “Enough! You are both winners, and the prizes will be equal.”

Next came a footrace among three runners: Ajax the Less, Ulysses, and Antilochus. Soon Ajax the Less was in front, with Ulysses right behind him, as close as the shuttle is to the breast of a woman standing at the loom and weaving. He ran hard on his heels, stepping in his footprints before the dust could settle. As they neared the finish, Ulysses prayed to Athene to help him. Athene heard him and made his knees and feet light and quick, and right at the end she made Ajax slip in the filth where some oxen had been slaughtered, so that his mouth and nostrils filled with it. So Ulysses won the mixing-bowl, while Ajax stood spitting the filth out of his mouth. He laid his hand on the head of the ox and cried, “The goddess made my feet slip, I’m sure of it, because she always stands by Ulysses and helps him, the way a mother helps a child.”

He said this, and everyone laughed to hear it. Antilochus came in last, taking the third prize. He said: “You know well, my friends, that the immortal gods always favor the old. Ajax is only a little older than I am, but Ulysses belongs to an earlier generation. Still, his is a green old age, and hardly any of the Greeks can compete with him, except Achilles himself.”

So the Games of Patroclus came to an end. The people scattered to the ships, sat down to eat and drink, and afterward went to sleep. But Achilles did not sleep. He remembered his dear Patroclus and all the two of them had done and suffered together, traveling over sea and land and standing against the enemy on the day of battle.

chapters.title: The Ransoming of Hector
paragraphs: When Patroclus had been buried, the gods held a council about Hector. Achilles was still dishonoring Hector’s body by dragging it around his friend’s tomb, but the gods pitied the dead man, because in life he had always honored them.
Then Zeus sent for Thetis, and when she came to Olympus he said: “Go to the camp and tell your son to give Hector back for a ransom. I am angry with him, because he dishonors the dead.”

So Thetis went to Achilles and found him weeping quietly for his dead friend, since the force of his grief was now spent. She said to him: “The gods want you to give up Hector’s body and accept in exchange the ransom of gold and precious things that his father will bring you.”
Her son answered, “So be it, if the gods want it.”
Then Zeus sent Iris, his messenger, to King Priam. The old king sat with his face wrapped in his mantle, his sons weeping around him and his daughters wailing through the rooms of his palace.

Iris spoke: “Take heart, Priam. Zeus has sent me to you. Go, and bring with you the gifts most likely to please the heart of Achilles, and carry home the body of your dear son Hector. Go without fear of death or harm, and go alone. Only let an old herald go with you, to help you when you bring back the body of the dead.”

Priam rose joyfully and told his sons to bring out his chariot. But first he went to his chamber and called his wife Hecuba and told her what he meant to do. She tried to talk him out of it, but he paid no attention. He said: “Do not try to hold me back, and do not be a bird of ill omen in my house. If a prophet or seer had told me to do this, I would have thought it a deception. But now I have heard the very voice of the messenger of Zeus. So I will go. And if I die, what do I care? Let Achilles kill me, if only I can hold my son’s body in my arms once more.”

Then he ordered that these be loaded into a wagon: shawls and mantles that had never been washed, along with rugs, cloaks, and tunics, twelve of each; ten talents of gold; two bright three-legged cauldrons; four basins; and a cup of rare beauty that the Thracians had given him. The old man held nothing back, if only he could buy his son back. He would not allow any of the Trojans to come near him. “Go away,” he cried, “you cowards! Don’t you have anything to mourn at home, that you come to mourn with me? You will be easy prey for the Greeks now that Hector is dead.”

Then the old man climbed into his chariot in haste and drove out of the palace. In front of him the mules pulled the four-wheeled wagon, guided by the herald Idæus. The old king drove his own chariot. All his relatives went with him, weeping as if he were going to his death. But when they came down from the city to the plain, Priam and the herald went on toward the ships of the Greeks, and all the others turned back to Troy.
Zeus watched Priam set out, and he told Hermes: “Take King Priam to the Greek ships, and guide him so that nobody spots him until he is at the tents of Achilles.”

Hermes tied on his feet the beautiful golden sandals in which he flies, as fast as the wind, over sea and land, and he took in his hand the rod with which he closes and opens men’s eyes as he pleases. He flew down and landed on the plain of Troy, taking the form of a handsome young man.

But when they had driven past the great Tomb of Ilus, they stopped the horses and mules to let them drink from the river. Darkness fell over the land, and then the herald caught sight of Hermes and said:—
Her’-mes.
“Think, my lord, what we should do. I see a man, and I am terribly afraid he will kill us. Should we flee in the chariot, or go up to him and beg him to have pity on us?”
The old man was badly shaken, and his hair stood on end with fear. But Hermes came up, took him by the hand, and said:—

“Where are you going, old man, with your horses and mules through the dark? Aren’t you afraid of these fierce Greeks, who are close by? If anyone saw you with all this wealth, what then? You aren’t young, and neither is your attendant, so you could not defend yourselves against an enemy. But I will not hurt you, and I will not let anyone else, because you remind me of my own dear father.”
“You are kind, my son,” said the old man. “Surely one of the blessed gods is with me, to bring me together with someone as handsome and wise as you. Happy are the parents of such a son!”

Hermes said: “Come, tell me the truth, old man. Are you sending all these treasures away to be kept safe for you far from here? Or are all the men of Troy leaving the city, now that they see Hector, their bravest warrior, is dead?”
Priam answered, “Who are you, my son, and who are your people, that you speak so truly about my unhappy son?”

“I have often,” said Hermes, “seen Hector in battle, both at other times and when he drove the Greeks back to their ships. We stood and watched and marveled at him, because Achilles would not let us fight, being angry with King Agamemnon. Now I am a follower of Achilles, and I came from Greece in the same ship as he did.”
Then Priam said, “If you are an attendant of Achilles, tell me the truth: is my son still by the ships, or have the dogs eaten him?”

Hermes answered, “Neither dogs nor vultures have eaten him. He still lies beside the ships of Achilles, and although this is the twelfth day since he was killed, his body has not decayed at all. Even though Achilles drags him around the tomb of his dear Patroclus, nothing ugly has marked him. He lies there fresh, the blood washed from him and all his wounds closed—and many spear-points pierced him. The blessed gods love him dearly, dead as he is.”

King Priam was glad to hear this. “It is good,” he said, “for a man to honor the gods. My son never forgot the gods of Olympus, and now they have not forgotten him, even in death. But take this beautiful cup as my thanks, do me this kindness, and lead me to the tent of Achilles.”

“No,” Hermes replied, “you offer it in vain. I would not take any gift from your hand without Achilles knowing. I respect him greatly, and I am afraid of robbing him, in case something bad happens to me later. But I will guide you all the way to Argos, if you wish, by land or by sea, and no one will blame me for guiding you.”

Then he jumped into the King’s chariot, took the reins in his hands, and gave the horses and mules a strength that was not their own. When they reached the ditch and trench that protected the ships, the guards were busy eating their meal. Hermes put them to sleep, opened the gates, and brought Priam in with his treasures. When they reached the tent of Achilles, Hermes stepped down from the chariot and said:—

“Look, I am Hermes. My father Zeus sent me to be your guide. Now I will leave, because I do not want Achilles to see me. But you go in, clasp his knees, and plead with him in the name of his father, his mother, and his child. That way you will move his heart to pity.”

So Hermes went back to Olympus, and King Priam jumped down from the chariot. He left the herald to look after the horses and mules and walked to the tent. There he found Achilles sitting. His comrades sat apart, but two of them were waiting on him, since he had only just finished his meal and the table was still beside him. No one saw King Priam until he was right next to Achilles. Then Priam caught his knees and kissed his hands, those dreadful, murderous hands that had killed so many of his sons. Achilles was amazed to see King Priam, and his comrades were amazed too, and looked at one another. Then King Priam spoke:

“Think of your father, godlike Achilles, and pity me. He is old, as I am, and perhaps his neighbors trouble him because he has no one to defend him. Yet as long as he knows you are alive, he is content, because every day he hopes to see his dear son come home from Troy. But I am completely miserable. I had many brave sons—nineteen born to me by one mother—and most of them are dead. The one who was best of all, who kept our city safe, has been killed by you. He is the one I have come to ransom. Have pity on him and on me, and think of your father. Surely no one has ever suffered a lot as sad as this: to kiss the hands that killed his son.”

These words stirred the heart of Achilles so deeply that he wept, thinking first of Patroclus and then of his old father at home. Priam wept too, thinking of his dead Hector. But at last Achilles stood up from his seat and lifted King Priam up, taking pity on his white hair and white beard, and said:

“How did you dare to come to the ships of the Greeks, to the man who killed your sons? You must have a heart of iron. But sit down. Let us keep our sorrows quiet in our hearts, since there is no good in mourning. It is the will of the gods that men must suffer, while they themselves are free of care.”

But Priam answered, “Do not make me sit, great Achilles, while Hector lies unhonored. Let me ransom him and see him with my own eyes, and you take the gifts. And may the gods grant that you return safely to your homeland.”

Then Achilles hurried out of his tent, with two comrades behind him. First they unhitched the horses from the chariot and the mules from the wagon. Then they brought in the herald Idæus and took the gifts. They kept back only two cloaks and a tunic, to wrap the dead man in. Achilles told the women to wash and anoint the body, but away from the tent, so that Priam would not see his son and cry out. When the body had been washed and anointed, Achilles lifted it in his own arms and laid it on the litter, and his comrades lifted the litter onto the wagon.
When everything was done, Achilles groaned and called out to his dead friend:

“Do not be angry, Patroclus, if you hear in the unknown land that I have given Hector back to his father for ransom. He has paid me a noble ransom, and you too will have your share of it, as is right.”

Then he went back to his tent and sat down across from Priam. He said, “Your son has been ransomed, old man. Tomorrow you will see him and take him back to Troy. But now let us eat. Tomorrow you can weep for Hector.”
So they ate and drank. When the meal was over, Achilles sat marveling at King Priam’s noble look, and King Priam marveled at Achilles, who was so strong and handsome.
Priam then said, “Let me sleep, great Achilles. I have not slept since my son fell by your hand. Now I have eaten and drunk, and my eyes are heavy.”
So Achilles’ comrades made him a bed outside, where no one could see him. If any of the chiefs came to the tent of Achilles to talk over plans, they might notice him and tell King Agamemnon.

But before he slept, King Priam said, “If you are willing to let me bury Hector, let there be a truce between my people and the Greeks. For nine days we will mourn for Hector. On the tenth we will bury him and feast the people. On the eleventh we will raise a great tomb over him, and on the twelfth we will fight again, if we must fight.”
Achilles answered, “So be it. I will hold back the war for that long.”

But while Priam slept, Hermes, the messenger of Zeus, came to him and said, “Are you sleeping, Priam, among your enemies? Achilles has accepted ransom for your Hector, but your remaining sons would pay three times as much for you, if Agamemnon learned that you were among the ships.”

The old man heard him and trembled. He woke the herald, and the two of them harnessed the horses and mules. They passed through the army, and no one knew. When they reached the river, Hermes went back to Olympus, and morning shone over the whole earth. Wailing and weeping, they carried the body to the city.

At once every man and woman in the city came out. They met the wagon close to the gates, with Hector’s wife leading the way and his mother and the whole crowd following. They would have stayed there weeping and wailing until evening, but King Priam spoke:
“Let us through. You will have plenty of time for wailing once we have taken him home.”
So they took him home and laid him on his bed. The minstrels sang their laments, and the women wailed.
First of all came Andromache, his wife, who cried:

“O my husband, you have died young, and I am left a widow, and our child, yours and mine, is only a baby! I fear he will never grow to be a man. Before that day comes, this city will fall, because you are gone, and you were its defender.”

Next Hecuba, his mother, spoke: “My son, you were dear to the immortal gods in life, and you are dear to them in death. Achilles dragged you around the tomb of his dear Patroclus, but he could not bring Patroclus back. And now you lie fresh and fair, like one the god of the silver bow has killed with a sudden shot.”

And last of all came Helen, who cried: “Many years have passed since I came to Troy—I wish I had died before then! In all that time I never heard one bitter word from your lips, and when others spoke harshly to me, you stopped them with your kind words. So I weep for you. No one is left to be my friend in all the broad streets of Troy. Everyone avoids and hates me now.”
And all the people wailed in answer.
Then Priam spoke: “Go, my people, and gather wood for the funeral. Do not fear any ambush from the Greeks, because Achilles promised to hold back the war until the twelfth day comes.”

So for nine days the people gathered a great deal of wood, and on the tenth day they laid Hector on the pile and lit a fire beneath him. When it had burned down, they put out the embers with wine. Then his brothers and comrades gathered the white bones and laid them in a golden chest. They covered it with purple robes, put it in a great coffin, and piled many large stones on top. Over all of it they raised a mighty mound, and all the while watchers kept guard in case the Greeks rose up and killed them. Last of all, a great feast was held in King Priam’s palace.
That is how they buried Hector.
After these events Achilles himself died. He tried to break through the Scæan gate, and there Paris wounded him fatally with an arrow, though it was Apollo who guided the archer’s hand.

Troy still could not be taken, so the Greeks pretended to leave, burning their camp and sailing away in their ships. But they left behind a great wooden horse, with the bravest of their chiefs hiding inside it. The men of Troy dragged it into their city. That night, while they were feasting, thinking the war was over, the chiefs climbed out of the horse and threw open the gate, and the Greeks poured in and took the city.
